Mr. DOHERTY moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 213, to amend the Dominion Lands Act. He said:
The purpose of this Bill is to meet a condition that may be created by the passage of the Naturalization Bill, which is now before the House. By reason of the change in the new Bill as to the period of time required for naturalization, those who have taken up homesteads may find themselves at the end of the three years not in a position to get their patents because of their not yet being British subjects. This Bill contains but one section, which provides that a homesteader who has made entry before the coming into force of the new Naturalization Act, and who would be entitled to his patent under the law as it now stands, upon declaring his intention to become naturalized as soon as he is in a position to comply with the requirements of the new Act, shall be entitled upon that declaration of intention to receive his patent just as if he were a British subject.

On the Orders of the Day being called:
I would like to repeat the inquiry of yesterday in regard to what has taken place in connection with the recent arrival of Hindu immigrants at Vancouver.

We have not had any word since yesterday; in fact, I do not think we had any word at all yesterday or to-day. The vessel is about one-half mile from the Port of Vancouver and the immigrants are being examined as to their physical and
mental condition under the provisions of the Immigration Act. We have not had any word to the effect that that examination has as yet been concluded.

May I also repeat the inquiry which I made yesterday of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) as to whether it is the intention of the Government to take action under the section of the Immigration Act that excludes action by the courts until the immigrants have been finally landed or passed by the Immigration Department? Does the Government intend to maintain that jurisdiction to the exclusion of the courts?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker, from information I have received I deem it my duty to call the attention of the hon. minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) to the condition of the Printing Bureau. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In reference to the noise in the House, and the large number of members constantly moving around, a complaint has been made to me more than once by the reporters that they find it very difficult to hear what is being said. They suggest as a remedy for one of these difficulties that members, especially ministers, should speak a little louder, and as a remedy

On the motion of Mr. Borden for the second reading of the proposed resolutions respecting the Canadian Northern Railway Company:

Mr. Speaker, before the motion is carried I would like to make a few observations on this very important public matter. It was my intention to say something about this question on the second reading of the Bill, but having just been in my county I have some idea of the public sentiment in regard to this matter which I think I should communicate to this House. This is one of the most important questions that has come before this Parliament since I have had the honour of a seat in it. The Dominion Government, at the present time, is taking upon itself in these resolutions a liability of $45,000,000. The Government of the day is well aware that a time of falling revenues, when owing to extravagance the public expenditure is being increased and the public debt also, is the time when a matter of this kind should be dealt with in all seriousness and when the public interest of Canada should at least be protected. Prior to the opening of Parliament this session, various rumours appeared in the press- in regard to assistance that was to be given to the Canadian Northern by this Government. Those rumours were very persistent, and they varied in some degree from time to time as- the press apparently got hints from members of the Government as to what form that assistance would take. I found, in talking over this matter with not only Liberals but Conservatives, that there was- only one view throughout that part of western Ontario from which I come, and that was that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, although they may be men of daring and of financial ability, and although they may be great railway contractors-, have received from the people of Canada all that any men should receive in the form of public assistance. There has been great doubt in the minds, not only of Liberals, but of Conservatives, in western Ontario as to the advisability at this time of assisting these men in the manner in which the Government is proposing. More than that, there is amongst the ordinary electors of western Ontario the most resolute resistance to this resolution (with

the exception of the resistance to the naval measure of last year) that I have met with since I have been in public life. These men have bled the municipalities, the provinces-, and the Dominion of Canada; and I must say that, amongst Conservatives and Liberals alike, there is only praise given to the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) and the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) for the independent and patriotic stand they have taken with regard to these resolutions.
It is only my intention to discuss these resolutions in a general sense, not to go through them seriatim. When I came to the House this session I was confirmed in my view that the voice of the people as pronounced in western Ontario was correct. I am not one of those who believe that the voice of the people is always the voice of Providence; but I think the voice of the people in a case like this is a pretty safe guide as to the proper course for the Government to take. When I came to the session, I thought that the good common sense of this House would prevail to some extent, and I was rather delighted to find the public opinion existing in western Ontario confirmed by so many members of this House on both sides. In the first place, we have the public opinion of western Ontario resolute against this measure. In the second place, let us take the hon. member for Kingston-and there is no better Conservative than he in this country-a man who has shown an independent spirit in provincial politics and who has to-day shown it in Dominion politics, a man with whom I was acquainted in college days, and whom I know intimately, a man who is moved only by patriotism-I find him with his face set against this measure. He has had large business and political experience, and it must have been a struggle for him to depart from his party on this measure; and yet I find him confirming the views of the people of western Ontario as I understand them. The hon. member for Calgary is one of the most eminent railway barristers in Canada, a man of wide railway experience, a man known throughout the West as a man of sound judgment and business acumen, and one who is not the least of the Conservatives in this House; I find him also with his face set against these resolutions. He has described these men as political mendicants, and I think his description is absolutely correct. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, in my opinion, have been the most persistent pair of political parasites with which any country has ever been afflicted.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will deal with the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton)?
I may deal with him later on.
Deal lightly with the erring one.

Let us take the other side first. I have not heard my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) say anything in regard to these resolutions, but he was not so silent during the last Parliament. What has happened him?
We go down the line and we come to the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), whose fidelity to Conservative principles no-one will doubt because he is the high prieBt of protection and of all the doctrines that go to make up Conservatism. What does he say in regard to these resolutions and these people to whom we are proposing to grant this aid? He says, just as, the hon. member for Kingston said, that they are not to be trusted. He says ' A burnt child dreads the fire '; he says * When you are supping with the devil, you must use a long spoon'; and therefore it is apparent that the hon, member for St. Antoine has not too much faith in the men with whom this Government is dealing.
Then we come to the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). He describes the operations of these men, if I remember aright, as, rather buccaneering operations, and so it is apparent that he has not much confidence in these men to whom the country is going to grant assistance to the extent of $45,000,000.
Then we come to the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Garrick), who is a personal friend of mine. He delivered an excellent speech on this matter. Of course, he admitted that these were his friends and that he was interested. I am not surprised at that for I thinlc that probably he is; but he seems to think that some more members on the Conservative side of the House are against these resolutions, than those who have voted against them. He seemed to express doubt in regard to-the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Hepburn) who, he said, was unanimously elected chief whip of the new Bull Moose party, which comprises the Conservatives who are opposing these resolutions. He expressed doubt even as to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins), wno is also a high priest of Conservatism.
'Then we come to the right hon. the Prime Minister. He evidently has some

doubt himself as to the fidelity and honesty of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, who are seeking relief, because he telle us that he had a statement last session from a high official of this company that $15,000,000 would complete the road, showing that he, the Premier of this country, having once been deceived by these men, he should, as the hon. member for St. Antoine says, use a long spoon when supping with the devil.
I am not at the moment aware of having said that, but perhaps I may be in error.

I certainly apologize if 1 have misrepresented what the Premier said; but I understood that, in answer to a question on the Order Paper, the Premier said he had been told by a high official that $15,000,000 would be sufficient to complete this road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my statement related to the ability to complete the road without assistance under ordinary financial conditions.

Well, it is practically the same thing. The right hon. gentleman understood, and I think it was the general impression left upon the House by his statement of last session, or by the general discussion of last session, that $15,000,000 would be sufficient to complete the road.
The greatest offender of all in this respect is the hon. Minister of Finance. He is the guardian of the public purse of this country. He has been in this Parliament for three sessions, and in his modest way he has claimed on various occasions to be a splendid accountant, to be able to diagnose a balance sheet as well as any man in the House or in the country. He has told certain members on this side that they were not mathematicians, leading us to believe, inferentially, that he was a mathematician. He has even said to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that that hon. gentleman should not doubt his legal knowledge because he had some legal knowledge. So, in this case we may not have ' a ministry of all the talents ' but we have a minister of all the talents. He is mathematician, Finance Minister and lawyer. Yet, if there is anything that has happened this session that should lead the Government to go slow in this guarantee, it was the discovery of the Finance Minister's action in relation to these contractors. Last session we advanced to this

concern the sum of $15,030,000 which was supposed to go into the construction of the Canadian Northern railway. The Minister of Finance told us, as the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) pointed out, that the Canadian people were getting ten per cent of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway for the $15,000,000 that we were giving them in cash. He stated that in four different places. You will find it recorded, for instance, at page 11725 of ' Hansard ' of last year. This statement was made in answer to a question by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy):
Yes. Therefore, taking the whole capital stock-
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, not the stock issued, but the whole capital stock.
-of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which controls 4,500 miles in the West, and owning, I believe, the Canadian Northern Quebec system, and affiliated with the other systems with the ultimate idea of amalgamating them all into a system extending over the continent, the Dominion owns one-tenth of that stock.
What docs that mean? The entire capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway was $92,000,000. But as a result of this arrangement of last session we got only $7,000,000 of stock. The minister led us to believe that we were getting ten per cent of the whole capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway as I have read you from ' Hansard'. Now, either as guardian of the public purse of Canada, this minister of all the talents was derelict in his duty and guilty, as he would say s in common law,' of negligence, and so lost to usi $2,200,000 worth of stock, or else he was deceived by these men whom we now find before Panldament for further assistance. Either his arithmetic was bad, or his .law was bad, or his faithfulness so far as public duty was concerned was worse. Such being the case, after listening to the debate in this House and listening attentively, after discussing the matter with the people in my part of the country and hearing the expressions of opinion both on the other side of this House and on this, I have come to the conclusion; that these applicants are men with whom the Government should enter into an arrangement only after the closest investigation and scrutiny of the facts. I have listened in this House to questions asked of the ministers generally as to the meaning of these resolutions and to the replies given to those questions. Listening to the
MAY 23, 19i4
reply given by the Solicitor General as to the meaning of section 14, I confess that- amd I do not wish to say anything offensive -not only did I not learn what that section meant, but I doubt very much if the hon. gentleman himself knows what the reason is for that clause being incorporated in these resolutions. It seems to me that in this matter the Solicitor Generali has taken up a new role. It seems to me he is not here to protect the public .interest in this guarantee transaction, but that he is here as counsel for Mackenzie and Mann. Everything he says tends towards that. His answers may be summarized: It .is not going to hurt the public interest and Mackenzie and iMann want it. It looks a.s if section 14 and others had not 'been drafted by the Solicitor General but had been put there by other hands than his, hands more crafty, and directed with greater knowledge of the intricacies of acts of this kind, and with the set purpose of placing upon, the people of Canada a burden from which they will [DOT]not be free for many years to come.
What was actually done in this matter so far as investigating the facts is concerned? On what evidence are we asked to grant this aid?
We have the officers of the Railway Department making an investigation at the instance of the Government. I say nothing of the competence or incompetence of these officers, for I know nothing about it. But it seems to me that a full investigation made by officers of the Department of Railways of all the intricate dealings of Mackenzie and Mann in the course of twenty years could not be made in the length of time that these officers have taken for that work. I assume, of course, that these men were sent there with instructions from the Government to get at the bottom of things. But, knowing what the Government was going to do or was likely to do, their investigation would be superficial and would only go to confirm the statement of the officers of the company themselves. In the second place, it would seem to me that the affidavits we have received in regard to what has been done by these men with the money they have received and with regard to their general financial situation, are very unsatisfactory. I do not know what relations exist between the hon. member from Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and Mr. A. J. Mitchell, and I have no reason to doubt the honesty of Mr. Mitchell, but my hon. friend from Norfolk spoke of this gentleman in a rather fatherly way as if he believed every-276
thing he said, and appeared to me in his action in this matter to be' influenced rather by personal than by public grounds, but in Mr. Mitchell's declaration all he said was ' to the best of my knowledge ' and ' judging from the books of the company.' But when Mackenzie and Mann come and ask a guarantee from this country of 545,000,000 of their bonds, the least they can do is to come to this House and submit their own affidavits with regard to the facts. I know of no reason why Sir William Mackenzie is not a proper person to make an affidavit. And I say the same concerning Sir Donald Mann. Why cannot these men submit their own affidavits that they have received no personal gain from the grants made to the Canadian Northern railway by this country ? If I were to go to the bank for a loan, the bank would not expect a statement from a student in my office, but would ask me to make a personal declaration as to the value of my assets. And in the next place, you will notice that the declaration of Mr. Mitchell was taken before Mr. Z. A. Lash. That seems to me almost improper,-it is in bad taste at the least. If the Government wish to accept a declaration of this kind, it should be made before some impartial party, and certainly not before a man so closely connected, as solicitor and partner with Mackenzie and Mann as Mr. Z. A. Lash.
Now, what security are we getting in regard to this guarantee and what investigation has been held as to that security ? In the first place we are getting all the physical assets of the Canadian Northern railway and also certain stocks on which grave doubts have been cast by members in this House, particularly by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett). He has told us that several of these companies have not paid interest on their bonds. That seems to be another reason for making an investigation before this grant is made. If these companies are in a practically bankrupt state their stock is no good. Attention has been called to the fact that we get no personal security from Mackenzie and Mann. And now, I am going to speak in a plain business way, as I have found business transacted in my part of the country. Mackenzie and Mann are no better tjian ordinary business persons in this land, any man in this House, or any other, and particularly the lawyers in this House, will know as a matter of business practice what happens if he goes to the bank to get a loan. I think Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann should be made subject to the



ordinary business principles that guide the bankers of this country. They have been here before; they have been treated generously; they have made a failure of the enterprises they have undertaken. They have been heralded throughout this country as two of the multi-millionaires of this land. I saw not long ago a report in a newspaper in which ten millionaires of Canada were mentioned, and high up in the list I saw .the names of Sir Donald Mann and Sir William Mackenzie. I do not begrudge them their wealth; I hope that they will have a great deal of it, but when they come to the people of Canada and ask for a guarantee of $45,000,000 on their bonds they should be made to follow the ordinary business principles of the average business man. No personal covenant is given by these men; no pledge is given of their personal assets except that they undertake to transfer to the Government a certain amount of stock and that they forego the commission which they say they have earned in the carrying on of their business. For my part, I do not believe what is said by Conservatives here and elsewhere that these men have not made money out of the undertakings which they have carried on. They went into the business as poor men, and if, as it is said, they .are wealthy, I cannot see where they have made their money unless it has been out of the assistance given them by the people of Canada. An eminent lawyer, one very familiar with railroad enterprises, said recently that Mackenzie and Mann have made as much money out of these contracts as they could draw out with their two hands, and that the only reason why they did not make more is because they had not more than two hands. I believe it and I say that it is only fair that we should judge them accordingly to ordinary business principles.
We have a covenant here on the part of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, that they will reduce the floating debt of the Canadian Northern and that they will pay off temporary loans. As the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) pointed out, the covenant of a limited liability company may be worthless or it may be of some value. The Solicitor General was asked not long ago in this House if he had made any inquiries into the financial standing of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. As I remember his reply, he said that he had not, and it seems to me that in that respect he has been derelict in his duty. If this company is to give covenants to the Govern-

ment, we should know something about their financial standing. That is a first business principle; if you are taking a covenant from a person or from a company you should know what is their financial standing in order that you can ascertain whether the covenant they give is valueless or valuable. The present Government in less than thirty months have given these men $21,640,000 in cash. That is a large sum of money. They have been helped by every province in the land; they have made a failure of their enterprise, and they come back asking for an increase of their credit. What would happen if any limited liability company in Canada went to the Bank of Commerce or to any other bank in this country and asked that their line of credit be increased? Every lawyer and every business" man in this House knows what would happen. The manager would say: we gave you a line of credit of $30,000; you ask us to increase that line of credit to $50,000. What are your assets? That is the first thing he would find out; but this the Government has not inquired into in the case of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. The next question the manager would ask would be: Who are the directors of your company? If these directors will give a personal bond to the bank and guarantee the line of credit which I give your company, I will increase your line of credit from $30,000 to $50,000. There is no reason why the Government in dealing with large financial matters should adopt principles different from those adopted by a bank or a financial institution in dealing with financial problems of less magnitude. That is the practice adopted by every bank in Canada, at least in nine cases out of ten, unless the limited liability company is beyond reproach of any financial unsteadiness. I would like to ask the Solicitor General here and now: Has this Government ever asked these men if they will give their personal guarantee that this agreement will be carried out?
If the hon. gentleman has read the agreement he must have observed that a great deal was asked of these gentlemen and that a great deal more was received than ever was received before.

The Solicitor General is at his old tricks; he will not answer the question. I would like to have a fair, straight and frank answer from him. These men have given their personal guarantee only in regard to one thing: that they will transfer certain stock to the Government

and that they will forego their commissions, which it is doubtful they have
12 noon, ever earned. What I am asking the Solicitor General-and I will try to make it as .plain as the English language can make it-is: has this Government or the negotiator of this agreement ever asked that additional security be given in the shape of the personal guarantee of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann that the agreement entered into with this Government shall be carried out?

I may say again-and if the hon. gentleman does not understand me I cannot heln it-that a great deal more was taken than has been suggested by the hon. gentleman, and the Government believe that they have obtained as much as can be obtained and at the same time keep Mackenzie and Mann responsible for the success of the enterprise.
The same answer. The Solicitor General will not say that the Government has asked for this personal guarantee and I say that the Government has been most derelict in its duty.

I say that the Government have asked for a great deal more than the hon. gentleman has even suggested and have obtained as much as could be obtained and at the same time keep Mackenzie and Mann responsible for the carrying out of the enterprise in the public interest.

I do not consider that to be a direct answer to my question. These people, mendicants, the hon. member for Calgary calls them, surely have no right to say what the bargain will be with the people of Canada. If this Government had not been dealing with men who were their friends before the last election and who are their friends to-day, they would have asked for and obtained the personal guarantee of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann before one dollar of this guarantee should be given to them. I say that this Government is derelict in its duty in not compelling these men to give their personal guarantee.

Why did not the hon.
gentleman: insist on that when aid was given to the Canadian Northern under the late Government?

The hon. gentleman knows
why; he is endeavouring to draw a herring across the trail. He knows that we got a first mortgage for whatever we gave and 2761
that we got ample security, which he is not getting to-day.

If a first mortgage is
all that is required, why did the hon. gentleman in 1909, when the Government took a fourth mortgage a.- their security, not insist on obtaining the personal covenant of the Grand Trunk directors?

The hon. gentleman does not answer my question. His duty is towards the people of Canada to-day. He has set himself up far and wide to be the great servant of the people in more ways than one; to be the great servant of the people of the West in more ways than one. At one time it was thought that he was in favour of free agricultural implements, free wheat and a lot of other things in the interests of the great West, but since he has entered this Government he has become the Tory of Tories, the protectionist of protectionists. I am very much afraid that if the people lean upon him, as a member of this Government, for assistance in the future, they will be leaning upon a broken reed. Personal security should be asked for from these people. 1 do not care what previous governments did, I do not care what this Government did; but I say that they owe it as a duty to the people of Canada to see that these men, who are getting a guarantee of $45,000,000, give us the best security that this Government can get from them. This Government is the superior power; these men come here as suppliants, and if they will not give security, this Government should refuse to give thjs guarantee.
There are other grounds upon which I am not in favour of these resolutions. I do not think that sufficient protection is given the people of Canada. Mackenzie, Mann and Company are to have the $45,000,000. They are to have control of this road, apparently without any restraint, for three years. II do not think, in the Lfe, of past experience, with their lack of success, that this country is doing right in giving them a free band, nor do I think one director on the board will help us a particle. The Government are not doing right in giving them the money without provision in the resolution that they can be pulled up short in case they do not carry out the work of the railroad in a proper business-like manner for the next three years.
Another reason why I am opposed to these resolutions is that a very short time ago a very large deputation from all over

Ontario appeared in this House to ask assistance in regard to electrical radial roads. We all know that the great problem before the people of this country-to-day is to decrease the cost of food products, to see that the producer gets his goods to the consumer with the least possible expense. We in western Ontario believe that the building up of an electrical radial road system will be very helpful. The suspicion is very general in western Ontario that these people, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, who are not esteemed to be men of a very unselfish nature, are not any too friendly to the development of the radial railroads in western Ontario. I do not think that men who have in their hearts no sentiment but selfishness, who have nothing altruistic in their natures, and who, as we suspect, are trying to impede the building of radial railroads in western Ontario for their own selfish purposes, should be assisted as they are being by the people of Canada to-day. These being my views on this matter, feeling that these men have not given security as they should, feeling that they have not backed up this grant by their personal prominence, I .have much pleasure in moving, seconded by Mr. McCbig:
That all the words after 'that' be struck out and the following substituted:
That the consideration of the said resolutions be not further proceeded with until a committee of Parliament has fully examined into and reported upon the necessity for the aid applied for by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the extent to which such aid should be given to complete this system, and the nature and value of the secyrity to be taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) has repeated a great many of the arguments and has made a great many of the allegations that have been heard, with a good deal of reiteration, in the House during the past week or ten days. So far as his speech consists of reiteration of what we have heard many times, he will pardon me if I do not follow him; and I trust he will not regard me as lacking in courtesy towards him inasmuch as three-quarters of what he has said has been answered and answered very satisfactorily at least half a dozen times. He will agree with me that it would serve no good purpose that I should repeat the answers so often and so effectively given.
He has enunciated in his resolution a new policy, and 1 believe that we shall have others later on from hon. gentleman on his side of the House.

We had the announcement in the first instance from the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition that such steps must be taken by Parliament as would prevent this enterprise from collapsing and would insure the completion of the road. I am not quoting textually from what my right hon. friend said, hut I am giving as accurately as I remember the exact purport of his words. A similar statement was made toy the hon. merhber for South Renfrew, who went even further than the right hon. leader of the Opposition, and who said that not only must the completion of this road be assured in the interests of the country, but that its completion must not for one moment be delayed. And then these hon. gentlemen proceeded to give evidence of the sincerity of their statements, and of the consistency of their views with their votes, by supporting a resolution which would postpone for at least one year or eighteen months any aid which could be effective in securing the completion of the road. In other words, by their voice they declare absolutely, as distinctly as could be declared by men in this Parliament, that Canada must come to the aid of this enterprise; that its coming to the aid of this enterprise is in the interest of the people of all Canada, and that they were prepared to support a measure to that effect, although they disagreed with some feature.-, it is true, of the particular measure which we have presented to Parliament. Then, by their vote, they ask that consideration of the proposed resolutions shall be postponed for six months, which means that they could not be taken up until the next session of Parliament, and that no effective aid could be given for at least eighteen months while, in the meantime, the labourers and sub-contractors and material men and merchants throughout Canada, who represent an indebtedness of about $21,000,000, would suffer for want of their money, and the whole industrial life of this country be thrown into confusion.
My hon. friend for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) proposes something of the same kind, for if his resolution means anything it means that the work upon the Canadian Northern Railway system shall stop, that the organization shall be disbanded, that men shall be thrown out of employment by the thousand, and that the thousands of men, workmen and others, throughout this country to whom

legitimate debts are owing shall go without their money for eighteen months or more. It is the same proposal made by my hon. friend from Pictou, though in a somewhat different form. My hon. friend from West Middlesex is entitled to his opinion, but I desire to tell him here and now that I do not believe any considerable portion of the people of Canada are in favour of his policy. I believe that a vast majority of the people of this country consider that the completion of this road should not be put off indefinitely. I believe they are in hearty concurrence with the opinion of his own colleague, the hon. member for South Renfrew, that the completion of this road should not even be delayed, and that they regard it as absolutely essential that the work should go on and not be interrupted in the way my hon. friend proposes. That is my conception, and by and by we may have an opportunity of testing the opinion of the electorate upon that particular question.
My hon. friend has made some rather curious statements designed, I suppose, more or less for political effect, and in particular he has asserted, upon what authority I do not know, that Mackenzie and Mann, besides being guilty of the various high crimes and misdemeanours to which he has alluded in a general way, have declared themselves to be in opposition to the radial system of railways which has been proposed by the Hydro-electric Commission of Ontario. On what authority does my hon. friend make that statement?
I said that in western Ontario there was a very deep suspicion that such was the case. I have heard it repeated time and again by very influential men in western Ontario.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can tell my hon. friend that I have some information on that subject. I have been informed by one who knows infinitely more about that subject than he knows, or is likely to know about it in the near future, that the statement which he has just made is absolutely without foundation. So far as the Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern interests are concerned, they are not only not in opposition to that proposal, but it has their very hearty support, and will have their enthusiastic co-operation; and I absolutely believe that the information which has been given to me in that regard is thoroughly reliable.
My hon. friend is very anxious for an investigation. Let me point out the position of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the
House in this connection. In 1911, those who were at the back of the Canadian Northern came to my right hon. friend and asked him and his Minister of Railways to declare by Act of Parlament that the Canadian Northern railway had the status of a great national transcontinental road. Will my right hon. friend deny that? He will not. They asked something further at that time; they a.-ked that the Parliament of Canada, recognizing the Canadian Northern Railway system as having the status of a great national transcontinental Tail way, should guarantee the bonds of that road to the extent of $35,000,000 for the purpose of establishing its status as a transcontinental road, and to complete a very considerable portion of the line -about 1,000 miles between Montreal and Port Arthur. According to the statement of my hon. friend from South Renfrew, the very fact that those bonds were brought here and a guarantee of th=* Government asked for was sufficient evidence that those securities were not marketable and that the assistance of the country must be given. Did the Administration of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition make one single inquiry into the financial condition, of the Canadian Northern Railway system at that time? Is my hon. friend from West Middlesex able to say that it did?
They got a first mortgage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They got a first mortgage which, according to the statement of his own leader, must be regarded as absolutely valueless, because the securities mortgaged were not marketable without the guarantee of the people of this country. I venture to say now, as I have said before, that it can be demonstrated to the satisfaction of any reasonable man that the security which the Government is receiving to-day for its proposed guarantee is infinitely more valuable than the security which the late Government took in 1911, although we have not a first mortgage. Was any inquiry made into the financial situation of the road in 1911? Was the company or Mackenzie and Mann asked at that time: Why do you come to the Government for a guarantee; you say your securities are unmarketable without the guarantee of the people of this country, and you come to the Government for aid; what is your financial position; are you able to carry out this great project of building a national transcontinental Tailway; what assets have you, Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited; what moneys have you

put iuto the construction of this road; what profits have you made; what claims have you against the Canadian Northern? Was a single one of these questions asked of these men? Will my hon. friend from West Middlesex assert that any such questions were put to Mackenzie and Mann or that any information on that subject was vouchsafed to Parliament at' that time? He knows that he cannot answer that question in the affirmative. And to-day, after the present Administration has made the most careful and searching inquiry into all these matters, he asks, for the purpose of keeping thousands of men An Canada out of their money for the next eighteen months or two years, that a further inquiry .be made by Parliament. We have had an inquiry by auditors appointed by the Government of this country, the best men we could select. We have had inquiries made of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and of its officials; we have had inquiries made of the Canadian Northern1 Railway Company and its officials. We have had this matter looked into in the most effective and thorough way that seemed to us possible undeT the circumstances, unless we ware prepared to postpone the completion of this road for eighteen months or two years. We have done in that regard infinitely more than ever was thought of by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House when they bad a similar question before them. Under these circumstances my hon. friend asks that this question shall be considered further by a committee of Parliament. In addition to what I have already said, the question has already been considered by this House sitting in committee for about a week, and questions relevant and irrelevant have been asked without end and information on every possible point, so far as it could be reasonably and properly vouchsafed in the public interest, has been given, to hon. gentlemen onj the other side of the House. What then must be the opinion of this country and of this House under he circumstances? Simply that the motion of my hon. friend is put forward as a political move and nothing more. He is willing to sacrifice the interests of this country, as they would be sacrificed by his proposal, according to the statement of the hon. member for South Renfrew. He is willing to delay the completion of this road and to keep thousands of people throughout this country, to whom debts are owing, [Mr Borden. 1
out of their money for perhaps eighteen months or two years in order that the political interests of the party opposite might 'be advantaged. Under the circumstances, I do not think it is necessary for me longer to delay this House, and I ask it to mete to the resolution of my hon. friend the treatment which he himself in his own heart knows it deserves, and that is to vote it down by ami overwhelming majority.

When the
company with which we aTe now dealing comes for the fourth time in four years asking for the assistance of this country, when it has already been given in the last three years more than $60,000,000 and now asks for $45,000,000 more. I think everybody will agree that the motion which has been made by my hon. friend from West Middlesex is a very reasonable one, and that we should know exactly what is the status of the company. If, as stated by my hon. friend, the company came here as a suppliant pleading that they were stranded, that they had not another dollar to pay their creditors and labourers, I admit that there would be some reason for the warmth displayed by the right hon. gentleman, but I must remind my right hon. friend that such is not the position taken by the company. They do not appear before Parliament representing that they are unable to pay a cent to their creditors and the labourers who built the road, as asserted by my right hon. friend, who declares that unless this money is voted the men who have built the road will not be paid. That is not at all the position taken by the company. It is one of the covenants of this agreement that no portion of this $45,000,000 shall be used to pay the men who excite the sympathy and consideration of my right hon. friend. When my right hon. friend is so solicitous about the creditors and the labourers, has he seen to it that the money which he is asking Parliament to vote shall go to the payment of these creditors and labourers? Nothing of the kind. It is stated in so many words that it shall not go to these creditors and labourers and therefore the tears which were shed by the Prime Minister a moment ago were shed in vain. It has been stated that not a dollar of this money is to go for the payment of the creditors and the labourers. Then what is to be done with the money that we are asked to vote? It is to enable the com-

panies to go on with their operations and to complete the building of the road. We can therefore, thrust aside the sympathy which the Prime Minister endeavoured to arouse when brought to close quarters in the consideration of this resolution.
But my right hon. friend has stated there is another reason. He asks: did the late Government ask for an inquiry when they gave the Canadian Northern Railway Company a guarantee to the extent of $35,000 a mile for the road from Port Arthur to Montreal? We have heard that argument before. That is the sort of argument that my right hon. friend undertakes to present whenever he is brought to close quarters- you did the same; you are another! We did not ask for an inquiry in 1911, but should ask for an inquiry in 1913 when an addition to the guarantee of $35,000 a mile, which had already been given for the completion of the road from Port Arthur to Montreal was granted? Did -my right hon. friend ask for an inquiry when he gave that additional subsidy of $10,000,000 cash, or $12,000 a mile? No, he did not. He relied upon the ability of the company to complete the road, as we had relied upon the ability of the company to complete the road. The company came back in 1911, in 1912, and in 1913, and on the last occasion my right hon. friend thought that we should have an inquiry and he tells us that it was a most complete inquiry. My right hon. friend admits that conditions have changed; that they are not the same as they were last year. Last year he gave $10,000,000 to the company, without going into their business at all. This year, when they come back for further aid he said: this has gone far enough and we must have an inquiry.
He tells us that the inquiry that has been made is the best that could be made, that it is complete, and that everything that could be done has been done. It may be that it has been sufficient for my right hon. friend. My right hon. friend told my hon. friend from Middlesex that his argument had been answered five or six times during the debate. Of course, it may have been answered to the satisfaction of my right hon. friend, and those who follow him, but if my right hon. friend and his followers are satisfied, those who sit on this side of the House ought also to be satisfied with the inquiry that has been made. My hon. friend thought that there should be an inquiry. What kind of an inquiry did he have ? He appointed three officers of the Government to inspect the books of
the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I have nothing to say against the officers of the Government who were employed for this purpose; they may be very competent -I believe they are-but under such circumstances as these, when Parliament is asked to vote money that will bring the total aid granted to this company during the last four years up to $100,000,000 or more, does my right hon. friend mean to say that this kind of an inquiry should be conducted by the accountants of the Government and not by independent accountants ? Such an inquiry should be held, as would not only satisfy the right hon. gentleman and his followers, but would satisfy the public at large, the men who have to pay the money. Does he mean to say that the best inquiry has been made when it has been conducted by accountants of the Government and not by the best firms of accountants to be found in this country or any other country ?
The position taken by my hon. friend from Middlesex is perfectly reasonable. Why should there not be a parliamentary inquiry ? The only reason stated by my right hon. friend why there should not be such an inquiry is that it would delay the payment of the poor men who are the creditors of the company. That concession has been removed by the fact that the resolution does not provide for anything of the kind. We have been assured from the Treasury benches in the last five or six days, over and over again, that the inquiry which has been made by these accountants has been most complete, but we now believe it has not been as complete as we had reason to expect. We have reason to believe that it has been far from complete. What information have we as to the value oi the securities placed before us ? We have simply the report of the accountants based upon the books of the company, and nothing more. What information have we in the report of the accountants, that has been laid on the table, that we have all the securities to which we are entitled? I asked a few days ago about the Niagara COmpany. I was told that there was no necessity for placing information on the table ot the House regarding the Niagara Company, because the Niagara Company belongs to the Canadian Northern, and therefore it is sufficient to have it so. That was the statement of the hon. the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), and we have no information from the accountants who were employed as to that. I submit that we should have had a far more complete inquiry, and that we should have had placed before us more detailed

information as to the securities which the Government are taking in consideration of this guarantee.
My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), some days ago, asked why we should not have the facts with relation to the Montreal Townsite Company placed before us, and why that company should not be included in these securities. The Solicitor General told us that he did not know anything about the Montreal Town-site Company. I looked at the book which has been placed before us, and I found that $5,000,000 of the $100,000,000 required to complete the enterprise is to be expended upon the Montreal terminals. We have to provide for the Montreal terminals, and yet we have no information as to the Montreal Townsite Company, which is connected with the terminals. We have to provide for the expenditure, and yet we have no information in regard to it. This illustrates the want of information that confronts us in dealing with an important question of this kind. What is the answer that the Solicitor General gave when he was asked for that information? This is the language which he used on that occasion :
Mr. Meighen : It would take a long time. They represent a great many assets, all the town-, sites acquired in connection with the lines in western Canada by Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, and all the agreements of sale and sums realized thereon.
Mr. Pugsley: Can the Solicitor General tell me in the name of what company these are held.
Mr. Meighen: The Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited.
Mr. Pugsley: That includes the most valuable of all, the townsite at Montreal?
Mr. Meighen:	I do not understand that
Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, own the site at Montreal.
Mr. Pugsley: Who does own it?
Mr. Meighen: I have no information to give the House on that point.
These so-called investigations were held, but we are told to-day by the Prime Minister in answer to the suggestion of my hon. friend the member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross), that we should have a full investigation on this point, that such an investigation will not be held because we already have a report upon this point. We have had an inquiry, the result of which shows on one side of the balance sheet $5,000,000 put down for expenditure on the townsite of Montreal; and on the other side, as regards any value that may come to us and the security of which will go to assist us, we are told by the Solicitor General that he does not care whether we have it or not; 
that he has made no inquiry whatever. My hon. friend shakes his head. Shall I repeat his words? Here they are:
Mr. Meighen:	I do not understand that
Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, own the site at Montreal.
Mr. Pugsley: Who does own it?
Mr. Meighen: I have no information to give the House on that point.
Mr. Pugsley : I may say that I do not think the Solicitor General ought to shut his eyes to knowledge which everybody else has.
Mr. Meighen: I do hot shut my eyes.
Later on he says this:
Mr. Meighen: If the hon. gentleman will show to the House that they own the townsite, I will undertake, on behalf of the Government, that it will be put in.
That is all the satisfaction which my hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) got from my hon. friend the Solicitor General. It was my hon. friend the member for St. John who was to get this information for the Solicitor General, and not the Solicitor General who was to get the information for the hon. member for St. John. In the face of that nothing can be more logical and to the point than that we should have a parliamentary inquiry.
My hon. friend tells me-and he relies upon me also-that I said in the opening of the debate that I did not want this enterprise to collapse. I repeat that I do not want this enterprise to collapse, but I certainly do not want it carried on in the manner provided by" my right hon. friend. My right hon. friend has stated that we object to some features of these resolutions. We object to the whole of the resolutions, because they are such as cannot be carried out to the satisfaction of the public and in the interest of the public. My right hon. friend says, with what intent I know not: I may appeal to the country upon this? I am dubious of the appeals of my right hon. friend to the country. He has told us many times that he is going to the country; but when the time comes, he puts it off to another day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that I would appeal to the country upon this.
I think my right hon. friend said that a moment ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not. I said that by and by there would be an opportunity of discussing this matter before the electorate, and that we would be willing then to discuss it.

In an election campaign we discuss things before the elect-

orate and get their verdict, but if this is simply to be an academic discussion before the public, that is a different matter. I have misjudged my right hon. friend, and I apologize; I have presumed too much upon his courage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The same kind of courage which my hon. friend showed in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Mr. Speaker, I do not
desire to engage the .attention of the House with a general discussion on the resolutions that are now before us for concurrence, and I shall attempt to confine myself to such features as have been called in question already in the debate. When the resolutions were first moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister., it was frankly stated that they were not placed here as immaculate and infallible but that we were open for suggestions as to improvements and for amendments in any way that might be devised in the public interest. That invitation has been very lightly accepted by many hon. members and suggestions have rained upon us almost without number. It must be admitted that if none of them appear to have any great force or to have any real amending value, they do not fail for lack of variety. There are some hon. members who, like the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), are anxious to do something and to do it now, and who suggest that it be done. There are others, like the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) and the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig), who want to do nothing. Then there are others who, like the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, are anxious both to do something a^d to do nothing. There are some who feel that we have not exacted sufficient from Mackenzie and Mann; that 40 per cent of an enterprise is not enough to exact in return for a bond guarantee of $45,000,000, the proceeds of which go into the enterprise. Those who take that view say that we should go further and increase that 40 per cent to 60 per cent or more, and thus gain control of the enterprise. Then there are some who,- like the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), say that we have gone far too far already, and that we should not take a dollar's worth of stock at all. Then there is the further suggestion of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) that we should'take a majority of the stock now; that we should get into the saddle and construct the road ourselves
a la the transcontinental construction;- that we should, while we are constructing it, switch Mackenzie and Mann off the track and operate the road, too, but that, as soon as we have it all done, we ought to reinstate Mackenzie and Mann in the control and operation of the road. Then there is the reverse position advanced by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who says that we ought to leave Mackenzie and Mann for the present in control of operation and construction to spend the $45,000,000, for which purpose they are quite suitable, until, say, within five years, they have it all done, and that then we ought to take it from them at a fraction of its value and operate the road ourselves. On the other hand, there are those who say that Mackenzie and Mann do not know anything about operation; that they are construction experts; but that when it comes to operation, they are mere children and no more competent to operate a railway than the waifs of the street. Then there are those who say that government operation is the last thing in the world, and who, like the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), frankly tell us that Mackenzie and Mann are good enough for them.
It will naturally be impossible for the Government to accept all these suggestions. One might go even further. There are some who take the view that we ought to proceed at once, and see the road through; that these are enterprising men, men of pluck and daring, deserving of assistance. That view is represented by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. There are some who have confidence in Mackenzie and Mann, who have expressed it throughout their careers and who are willing to abide by it, who believe that they are great Canadians, perhaps like all great men, not without faults, but who believe that they are great men and have made a better success of the Canadian Northern Railway sys-ten than we ourselves have made of the construction of the National Transcontinental. There are others still, who describe them as mere buccaneers, as mere parasites on the 'body politic-having become so just of late-and who would pursue them through twenty years of alleged crime from the time they stood on the banks of the Red river until they reached the waters of the Pacific.
Well, after all, the resolutions remain exactly as they were brought down. Three amendments have been moved, none of them embodying any of these virulent

and violent propositions enunciated by hon. gentlemen opposite-all very moderate resolutions, but unfortunately not in the public interest.
We come now to the position of the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross). That hon. gentleman takes the ground, that we ought to appoint a committee of the House to investigate the financial condition of the Canadian Northern railway and the value of the stocks and bonds of the (railway, its terminals, etc., before we proceed; which, being interpreted, means that we do nothing at all this session but that instead we wait till next and then start a committee going to investigate the accounting system and the value of the assets and securities of the concern. The leader of the Opposition has stated that the investigation we have made is not of much value.	True, be says, we appointed
accountants, the best in the Government service. One is the financial [DOT]comptroller of the Railway Department, a gentleman accustomed to this work for many years, and, if I am not mistaken, appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite. Another is a gentleman of similar position in the Finance Department, and another similarly situated in the Railway Department. These gentlemen have made an investigation. But, says the leader of the Opposition, it is true these men are competent, but they are not independent, and, being in the service of the Government they are likely to favour those with whom the Government is dealing. I should have thought that, if they had any bias, (being in the employ of the Government they would favour the Government, and that, being competent and honest men, their lack of independence would tell in our favour. He says that nothing but an investigation by outside accountants will suit him, and therefore he will support the amendment of the hon. member for West Middlesex whose proposition is to appoint a staff of competent accountants out of the House of Commons-doubtless he will call upon himself and the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and thus satisfy the leader of the Opposition that really competent accountants have investigated the Canadian Northern railway.
But the leader of the Opposition saye also: The argument you advance would be sound and I could not resist it if this money was really going to pay the debts of the concern; I could not

stand between the men who have built this road, whose labour and material have gone into the road after we had sanctioned it as a transcontinental system, but the trouble is they are not going to get their money out of this $45,000,000. The right hon. gentleman must have been absent from the House when this matter was under discussion, for it has been stated on the floor of this House and it is stated in the resolution itself, that the purpose of this guarantee is to complete the road. And how can the road be completed unless the money spent in building it is paid? We cannot take the road over from the contractor, noT can the Can-idian Northern railway, unless the debts against the road on construction account are discharged. Not only is that clear on the very face of the resolutions, but on the floor of Parliament and on behalf of the Government of Canada, with due authority for the words I used, I made the statement that the Government of Canada would see to it that the debts on account of construction as stated in the auditor's report would be discharged before the $45,000,000 was paid out. The right hon. gentleman has the undertaking of the Government of Canada on that point. Then, is not he bound, in justice to his own opinion as stated by himself, if he can remain consistent for half an horn;, to stand up and support the resolutions? These debts to- the amount of $21,262,527 are to be paid by reason of these resolutions going through, and will be paid before the money guaranteed is paid out. And we maintain control in the meantime. That removes the main obstacle to the support of the leader of the Opposition. But, he says, there is trouble yet over this Mount Royal tunnel situation. He says that $5,995,000 of this money is going to supply tunnel and terminal facilities at Montreal. He is mistaken; not one dollar of the $45,000,000 is going to supply tunnel and terminal facilities at Montreal. It has been stated on the floor of Parliament, times almost without number that that money is in sight and ready as soon as it is wanted. The financing was done temporarily by a firm of brokers in England, and, as they took all the risks of that project, the financing was done necessarily at a high rate of interest, relatively speaking. Eut, now that the venture is an assured success, arrangements have been made for the financing of the project at current rates, discharging these temporary bonds. All that appears cn the face of the returns laid on the

table. And, while hon. gentlemen complain so bitterly that we have not given them sufficient 'nforn. it.on, in the very words of their complaint they continually show that they have not taken in even a fraction of the information we have laid before them. The right hon. gentleman says we should have taken an interest in the Model City, a real estate speculation somewhere near Montreal, and because the Solicitor General refuses to tell the House who owns the Model City, and to state all the assets and liabilitiss of that real estate venture, the leader of the Opposition declares that he cannot see his way to support these resolutions. I did go to the extent of submitting to the House my opinion, as the result of inquiry made, that Mackenzie and Mann do not own that real estate speculation. But what is to be said of the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite, who declare in thunder tones throughout Canada that the Government must not link up with Mackenzie and Mann even to the extent of taking stock in a railway system in which Mackenzie and Matnm have stock; yet at the same time demand that we .shall enter into a partnership with them and several others in a real estate speculation somewhere near the city of Montreal? And the townsites are no good, either, according to these hon. gentlemen. I wonder what values the townsites would have had if we had not included them in our security. We should have had the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) picturing the almost fabulous value of the townsites near Edmonton. We heard the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) telling us the tremendous value there was in the townsite of Port Mann, if the Solicitor General had not been so mesmerized as to leave it out. But, as soon as he learned that it was in, he rose and said that it was of no more value than the village of Bossendale or any other little town on the line.
Now, the amendment before the House is not merely that we read these resolutions again this day six months-that would have satisfied the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), but it does not satisfy the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Boss)-but that everything shall be delayed until next session, and that then we shall appoint a committee of Parliament to investigate the financial condition of the road and try to find out whether we have enough security, or whether we had not
better adld some stocks in some Brazilian traction company or other assets, which, the hon. gentleman states, belong to these men, Mackenzie and Mann.
I have listened to many taunts from hon. gentlemen opposite, but. I do not think that I have anything to complain of. Certainly all the credit that is coming to me has been given me, if not a great deal more. I had something to do with these arrangements, but the Bill that is before the House derived its merit not from the humble individual who addresses you but from the fact that there are at the head of the Government of Canada to-day men who are able to deal with great affairs and solve the difficulties connected with them in the interests of the people. I do not pretend for one moment to measure up in legal experience or capacity to the distinguished man who represents Mackenzie and Mann in legal matters. I join with the hon. member for Pictou in paying tribute to the great ability of Mr. Lash. But the hon. member for Pictou should remember that in the negotiations I enjoyed this protection: that Mr. Lash well knew that whatever arrangements we might arrive at would be subjected to the scrutiny of really competent lawyers; that they would have to pass through this House; that they would have to pass under the eye of the hon. member for Pictou himself, and that there was no chance on earth that these resolutions would ever survive that furnace of fire unless they were ironclad against legitimate attack. Having enjoyed that protection, which, I know, must have had a restraining influence upon Mr. Lash, asking hon. gentlemen to keep in mind the fact that I was not wholly at his mercy, I leave the terms of the resolutions themselves to be the answer to hon. gentlemen opposite, or to hon. gentlemen not opposite, that I have been befooled, mesmerized, seduced, and all the rest of it in arriving at this arrangement with the Canadian Northern.
I have been charged by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Boss) with not knowing what the resolutions mean, and in order that he might make his charge in such a manner that no one could possibly dispute him, he really cited an instance. He tells the House: Here is a clause; I cannot tell for the life of me what this clause means, and the Solicitor General cannot either. I will read to the House clause 14 of the resolution, which he says is so inscrutable:
That no shares of the capital stock of the respective companies mentioned in the first sche-

dule hereto, other than the Canadian Northern, beyond the amounts heretofore issued, shall be issued without the consent of the Governor in Council,
I quoted the wrong section; it was section 19.

I asked the hon. member if it was section 14; he looked down at his paper and said it was. However, I do not know that 19 is any further from the A-B-C's than 14. It reads:
That any company now or hereafter comprised in the Canadian Northern system which is now or may hereafter be subject to the legis-receive advances from many other company corn-may acquire shares in the capital stock of, or securities issued by, or make advances to, or receive advances from any other company comprised in said system, and may take or give security for such advances.
Here is a system of companies, twenty-nine in number, the parent company being one; any one of them may make advances to any other and take security for them; any one of them may issue shares to another and pay for them or give value for them. They are enabled to take shares from each other if any object may be served thereby. I do not know what is so very mysterious about that; I do not know what is so very difficult to explain. The meaning of it is as clear as any sentence in the English language can be. I think what the hon. gentleman has in mind is this: that I did not pretend to be familiar enough with the actual operation and working of railway systems to be able to say just when and under what conditions this clause may be availed of. I did give some possible instances; that is all; does he expect me to be more? I tell him what the clause means; I tell him the extent to which it goes; I tell him its limitations; I show him that no public interest can suffer, and, with my meagre intelligence, I assume that my duty is then discharged. I trust that the hon. member for West Middlesex at last appreciates the meaning of clause 19.
