Mr. Speaker, I had understood that the Solicitor General had not concluded his remarks when the House rose for luncheon, and I am free to say that so far as my hon. friend had proceeded he had furnished to the House no reason why the amendment of my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) should not be accepted and ap-
proved. I was somewhat surprised at the attitude taken by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden.) in regard to this matter. One would have thought that the sole and only purpose of the Government in introducing this measure to Parliament was to enable certain people in this country who were owed money by the contractors for the Canadian Northern railway to be paid out of the treasury of the Dominion of Canada, and that the Opposition should be condemned and despised because they ventured to suggest that before assuming what will be ultimately a liability of $450,000,000, more than double the debt of the country, the House should pay this great measure, introduced at this late period of the session, the compliment of at least investigating the circumstances surrounding it and so enabling the country and Parliament to realize just where they stand in reference to it as a business proposition. The Premier knows very well that when the proposition to aid the Canadian Northern was first suggested during this session of Parliament my right hon. friend's position and that of the Government was that nothing should be done by way of loan to these gentlemen. I refer to the statement of the Minister of Finance in which he declared that the announcement made by Sir William Mackenzie in Toronto as to what was to be done by the Government had no foundation in fact; that he was not prepared to say what Sir William Mackenzie had said, but, so far as he was concerned, the statement that aid was to be given by way of loan was not a fact. Everybody knows that, were it not for the fact that these two astute gentlemen who are behind this project proceeded, as my hon. friend from Calgary pointed out, to lead this House and the Government to believe by representations to them through the men who were their creditors throughout the country, that a difficult situation existed, the Government would have not taken up this question at all and would not have asked Parliament to saddle this country with this huge and enormous liability. That being so, when the Government came to Parliament they did not come here asserting that they were asking this aid for this enterprise for the purpose of seeing that the creditors of this company were paid. Oini the contrary, the right hon. gentleman, in his opening address, asked Parliament to support this proposition because

it was the desire of the people who owned the various constituent companies to unite them together into a third transcontinental system, which the Government wished to see completed. That was the high ground upon which they came to Parliament. My right hon. friend asked Parliament to ratify this measure. Nothing was said about the payment of creditors and it was not said at that time that there were in this country a lot of people who were in financial difficulties on account of the	fact	that	they	had worked
for this company and had not been paid. No plea was put forward such as is being put forward to-day that you should not investigate this proposition at all because some people were out of money through their dealings with this company. My right hon. friend has descended from the high pedestal which he assumed in inaugurating this measure. Now the sole and only purpose of this measure is to see that certain gentlemen get their money and we are told that Parliament should assume, by virtue of the fact that we have become partners in this enterprise, a load of indebtedness which will more than double the public debt of this country. Therefore, I say let us take steps to see that the men who are entitled to get their money are protected; but before we assume this great liability, let us stop and investigate this thing. The question as to whether the men who have put their money into the work and material into the construction of this road should be paid is not an issue in this House. I can assure hon. gentlemen we would support any reasonable proposition which would ensure these men getting their money. That is one thing and the proposition that we should assume this huge liability without stopping to investigate is quite another thing. We say that before doing that, we should stop and investigate and that is the resolution of my hon. friend from West Middlesex. The Premier will not becloud the issue in the slightest degree by asserting vociferously, as he did this morning, that we should not take time to look into this thing in the smallest degree because there are some people to be paid. Let them be paid, but let us stop for a moment and consider where Canada will be ^fter they are paid. It is stated that there has been a full investigation. Was ever a more absurd proposition suggested to Parliament? What was investigated? What have we in these documents? We have here certain 'statements that were 'submitted by Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, prepared in their office and submitted to the Government. After they were submitted to the Government, the Government sent*certain auditors employed in the Civil Service to check over the statements and ascertain if they were added up correctly. That was the investigation that was made, nothing more and nothing less. These gentlemen who were authorized by this Government, went to Toronto and they asked Mr. Mitchell to produce the books of the company. He showed them the books and they checked off the items. Is that all that the country wants to know in regard to this enterprise before this liability is assumed? Is that a full and complete and adequate investigation such as any business concern in this or any other country would have made before assuming this enormous liability which is to be forever imposed on this country? Sir, it is a farce to come forward with such a suggestion as that. No investigation worthy of the name has ever been made into this matter nor does Canada know where she will stand when she assumes this liability upon which only time will throw light. My right hon. friend says that careful and searching inquiry has been made into the fact that men have been kept out of their money and he advances this as a reason why this amendment should not be adopted. Let me give two or three things that should have been investigated by the auditors that were not. In this bluejbook we find, o,n page 43, a statement of what is known as floating liabilities amounting to over $10,000,000. The largest item contained in it is one of over $6,000,000 from the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I asked my hon. friend the Solicitor General the day before yesterday to tell me what was included in that $6,000,000. My hon. friend has said that to the best of his information a certain portion of it had relation to moneys that had been paid out on equipment, but he could not say definitely in regard to the matter. He was also unable to give to the House the items which make up that $10,000,000.

Does not the hon.
gentleman know that floating liability simply means the current liability shown in the books of the company, and that it varies from day to day not only in its amount but as regards its apportionment between the creditors. I have already informed the hon. gentleman that this amount is largely due to the hanks for payments made in dis-

charge of the ordinary everyday liabilities of the company.

My hon. friend would dispose of it by saying that yiey are the everyday liabilities of the company, but the company has not floating liabilities to the extent of $10,000,000. They already owe to the 'bank $20,000,000.
No.
Yes, they do, for temporary loans.
That is right, I was not thinking of the temporary loans.

The Solicitor General has had no statement prepared by his auditors in regard to this amount, and he can give ns no information beyond what he furnished yesterday. No inquiry has been held as to whether these liabilities were properly or improperly contracted, as to how they originated, and whether that prudence has been displayed in the management of the railway which would warrant the country in taking notice of these liabilities. Take the item as to equipment trust. My hon. friend has succeeded admirably in beclouding the House and the committee as to where this concern stands in regard to equipment trust. The discussion that he and the hon. member for Calgary had in regard to this question was the inception of this beclouding of the issue. The hon. member for Calgary read from the report of the Canadian Northern Railway Company showing that it had a surplus of so much money, and the Solicitor General said that the surplus went into equipment trust, and he has been talking about equipment trust here and there all through this debate. Whenever my hon. friend could not explain an item he would say: Oh, that money has gone into equipment. In regard to this very item of $6,000,000, he said that a large part of it had gone ink* equipment. Do you not think it would be wise and prudent, Mr. Speaker, to have an investigation into this question of equipment trust? We have this condition: the Canadian Northern Railway Company gets its equipment through the Imperial Rolling Stock Company; the Imperial Rolling Stock Company gets it from Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited; and Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, purchase it from the car makers. It is the usual thing for railways to have a rolling stock company, but in other railways the equipment is purchased from the car makers in the first in-

stance and not through the medium of sub-contractors like Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. It would be most interesting if an investigation were held to ascertain whether Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, got any percentage on this equipment as it passed through their hands to the Imperial Rolling Stock Company.

The auditors have investigated that and found that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, made no profit on the transaction. In passing, may I say that the Intercolonial railway of Canada operated by this and the late Government buy some of the parts of their equipment direct from the makers instead of through the car trust, just as the Canadian Northern do because they can get it more cheaply that way. The makers of this equipment have adopted a system whereby they will sell portions of their equipment more cheaply directly to the railway companies than to the car makers, and that is the only reason why Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, bought the equipment themselves.

I repeat, how much more imperative does it become, from the standpoint of the good faith of the country, apart from any technical question of law, as to our partnership relations, after all that has been done, and after we agree to give this company a guarantee of $45,000,000 more on their bonds, that we should have the fullest information with regard to the affairs of the company? Why should we not investigate and find out the value . of the Inverness and Richmond railway, why should we not find out the value of these railways in the Niagara district, and of the radial railways running west from Toronto? Why should we not find out the value of the iron deposits and the iron works of these gentlemen up at Port Arthur, and why should we not find out the value of all the other various and widely-distributed interests of these gentlemen all over Canada? We say that we .should stop for a moment and ascertain these things, and if we find that the country can get more security before it doubles its debt, we should take it. l>o you mean to say that we should vote down a resolution which would bring about that good result? Yet that is the proposition of the Government and nothing more on this question.
Then my hon. friend the Solicitor General yesterday took a1 most singular position. He said that he did not regard it as being of any importance to the Canadian people what the assets and liabilities of this joint stock company, known as Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, were. In fairness, let us consider what is involved in that proposition. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are one of the important constituent factors in this whole proposition. They are called 'the contractors,' they sign the agreement, they become parties to the trust deed. In dealing with this railway proposition the Government say: we will not ask Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, to give us any statement of their affairs; we do not care whether they are bankrupt; we do not care what their last statement was, or whether their liabilities exceed their assets; to us it is a matter of perfect indifference. That is the position which my hon. friend the Solicitor General takes. He indicated that he had not even asked the joint stock company, Mackenzie, Mann and

Company, Limited, for a statement of their affairs. The logic of my hon. friend, from a business standpoint, cannot stand inspection for a moment. There are plenty of business men on both sides of this House. There is not one of them who is engaged in any active business in this country who would form a contractual relationship with any joint stock company in which the amount of the liability involved in that relationship amounted to $30,000,000, who would not ask the joint stock company to give him the last statement of their affairs, showing how they stood, which statement they would require to be certified by auditor s of probity about whom there was no question. Yet, the Government simply say: we will not ask; we do not think it is of any importance and we do not care.
Is there not ample room for an investigation in the interests of the country in reference to this important feature of the matter? Apparently that whole phase of the question has been disregarded by hon. gentlemen who undertake to tell us that there are some people in this country who are owed some money; therefore, disregard every other consideration, vote this whole proposition, impose this tremendous liability on the country, simply accept it and pay this $21,000,000. A singular feature in regard to this $21,000,000 is that the Government did not know whether it is to form part of the $100,000,000 until after this debate had gone on for three or four days. When I had the honour to speak upon the motion I made at the inception of this discussion, I asked the Solicitor General to let us know categorically and positively whether this $21,000,000 was to come out of the $42,000,000. The position my hon. friend took in regard to the matter is interesting. The forty-two million dollars ought to be the yield of the $45,000,000, leaving $58,000,000 besides that, and my hon. friend's position was this: it will come out of either one of them but I do not know which. After we had discussed this question my hon. friend went out and made it his business to find out where we were on the matter and he came to me a day or two afterwards and told me that he was able to give the assurance for the first time that the money would come out of the $42,000,000 or the $58,000.000. He does not even now take the position that the $21,000,000 is coming out of the $42,000,000. He simply takes the position as between the $42,000,000 and the $58,000,000 that as the Government are going to have something to do in regard to controlling the expenditure of this money, there will be

some place out of which that $21,000,000 will come.
Let me suggest to the House a possibility in connection with this matter. After this measure goes through and the parties who are disposing of these bonds go- to England, the first $45,000,000 of bonds which have been secured -by this guarantee, and which issue will he made in pursuance of this measure, will naturally be the securities which first will he sought after by any underwriters who want to deal with the matter. They will have to be sold first. The credit of Canada is good for $45,000,000 at this juncture, though what it will be in a year or two, if Providence permits this Government to remain in office, Heaven only knows. Forty-five million dollars may be sold, but where are they going to sell the $58,000,000? The London bankers will say: We will make you an offer for the $45,000,000, but we want to know about the $58,000,000. Part of it may be guaranteed by the provincial governments, but the rights of these provincial governments are being wiped out under this measure. Henceforth all legislation in regard to these railways that are now being declared to be for the general advantage of Canada must emanate from Ottawa. At this moment the particular section of the resolution relating to this matter stands suspended, like Mohammed's coffin, between heaven and earth. The local governments and the federal Government are unable to say just what the relation of the provincial legislatures is to be to these securities that are at present in existence. With that condition of affairs, are the gentlemen of the commercial markets of the world going to snap up the $58,000,000 worth of second-class securities? The consequence will be that the proceeds from this $58,000,000 will be delayed. Mackenzie and Mann, who will not say at this moment that they will pay their debts out of the $42,000,000, the supposed net proceeds of the $45,000,000, tell the men who are wanting this $21,000,000: When we are able to sell the $58,000,000 worth of bonds, you will get your proportion of it.

Would the hon. gentle-"man say what has become of the last clause of the amendment of which he gave notice?

I will explain that in a few minutes; or, perhaps, I had better refer to it now. After I gave notice to my right hon. friend the leader of the Government that I would move an 4 p.m. amendment in those terms, on further consideration I came to the conclusion that it would be desirable to strike out the last clause. By that clause, if the House had approved it, the Government would have been bound to leave the management of the road in the hands of the Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited. Upon fuller consideration I thought it would be better that the Government's hands should not be tied in that respect. By other provisions of the amendment, the full control of the company is vested in the Government, if the Government chooses to exercise the control. The amendment provides that the whole capital stock shall be vested in His Majesty for a period of five years. There would, of course, have to be enough stock in the hands of the directors to qualify them for their position, but the complete control would be in the hands of

the Government. If the Government thought right, they might leave that control in the hands of Mackenzie and Mann or their nominees.
As I have said, this amendment is in principle entirely opposed to the proposition put forward by the Government. I think we might well discuss it, apart altogether from any personal considerations, so far as Mackenzie and Mann are concerned. I would venture to hope that we might discuss it entirely aside from any partisan bias. For this is a question of enormous importance to the people of the country, not only to those who are living in Canada to-day, but to	those	who are	to comeafter those	who	are now uponthe stage	of	Canadian	affairs.The Government is proposing, most unwisely, I think, to go into partnership with Mackenzie and Mann. W-e know that iso far as the Canadian Northern railway is concerned these gentlemen started out with different ideas from those entertained by other great railway corporations both on this side of	the	Atlantic	and theother side. Ordinarily, when it is proposed	to	build a	railway,
there are two ways by which it is expected that means may be obtained for construction. One is by the issuing of securities and the proceeds of land grants, in case such grants should be made, and the other by issuing the shares of the company to form its capital stock. Hon. gentlemen know that there is to-day a very large amount of the capital stock of the Cam adian Pacific railway outstanding which represents money to a large amount that has actually gone into the construction of the railway. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann evidently started out with the idea that they would not allow the stock of the Canadian Northern railway to be circulated, would not place it upon the market, would not try to get people to invest their money in it and become shareholders with them in the enterpris-e, but wouild endeavour to construct the railway entirely out of Government subsidies, out of the proceeds of guaranteed bonds and out of the sale of lands which might be granted to them from time to time. Up to the present time they have held control of the entire capital stock of the company. That I am right in this appears from the return that has been laid on the table in which it is stated that the total issue of capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway is

$77,000,000 of which $7,000,000 is held by the Government under the .legislation of last session and $70,000,000 by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and their associates. Now it is proposed by the Government that His Majesty, represented by the Government and on behalf of the people of Canada, shall go into partnership with Mackenzie and Mann in this enterprise. It is very important to bear that clearly in mind. The condition of affairs to-day is in no way different from what it would be if they were just beginning this undertaking and the proposition were made to the Government to go into the undertaking and to engage in the construction and operation of a railway extending across the continent in which His Majesty would be represented by a two-fifths interest aind Mackenzie, Mann and Company by a three-fifths interest. That is what is proposed to-day. But the condition is even worse than it would be if we were at the commencement of the enterprise. The Canadian Northern Railway system has enormous obligations amounting to upwards of $300,000,000, the interest on which must be provided for. Under the management of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited-whether or not that management is to blame for it-this enterprise to-day is practically in a condition of bankruptcy. The Government say to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited: we are prepared now on behalf of the people of Canada to join with you and to become partners with you in this, undertaking; to bear with you its responsibilities and to share with you its profits. It makes no difference that the company in which they are to become a partner is an incorporated company. In former times companies were incorporated without a limited liability; in many cases they were organized without any incorporation at all. The only object of incorporation is that shares may 'be issued and distributed and the interest divided, and that there may be a liability limited to the amount of the shares held by each individual shareholder. The shareholders are exactly in the position of partners. They are obliged to share the losses, although they are not responsible to the public for losses beyond the amount of the stock which they hold, and they are entitled to a share in the ptofits in proportion to the amount of shares which are held by them. Although in this case His Majesty may say, through the Government of Canada: if this enterprise

goes down we do not hold ourselves responsible-just as Mackenzie and Mann might say 'because of the limited liability which is imposed by the statute incorporating the company-yet in all other respects the Government and Mackenzie and Mann are partners. So far as the management of the company is concerned, they are partners; so far as the right to share in the profits is concerned, they are partners. We are asked to authorize the entering into a partnership of the Government with Mackenzie, Mann and Company for the ownership and operation of this railway. It has been said that as the Government is in a minority, there will be no responsibility so far as the management is concerned. Sir, I deny that, the government of a country are in the position of trustees for the people whom they represent; the Government of this country are the trustees of the people of Canada and the moment they take property in this company, represented by stock of the par value of $40,000,000, having the right to vote for directors, having the right to have their nominees elected to the board of directors, the duty is cast upon them of watching carefully the interests of this company on behalf of the people for whom they are acting as trustees and of taking a part in its management. If that company goes to the wall, the people of Canada cannot escape the moral responsibility of standing behind the undertaking and seeing that people do not suffer through the operations of this railroad .in the future.
From what I have heard, I believe that among the business and financial men of this country and among the people generally, there is a determined and unalterable opposition to the Government's going into partnership with Mackenzie, Mann and Company in this enterprise. As I said the other day, if it is desirable to aid the Canadian Northern system, and I do not dispute that it is desirable, let that aid be granted upon its merits. The only sound reason for granting aid is that it is desirable that the undertaking shall be carried to completion so that we shall have another transcontinental railway extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Forty million, dollars of watered stock is to be laid away in the treasury in the expectation that at some time or other, through the tolls which will be paid to this railway company by the people o! Canada, there may be derived a revenue to the treasury of the Dominion. Surely that ought not to be a consideration influencing this Parliament and the people
of this country in approving the proposed action of the Government. Hon. gentlemen have argued that that is a great advantage; at the last session of Parliament the Minister of Finance put forward the same argument. He said: we are giving to the Canadian Northern Railway Company a bonus of $16,000,000 in cash, but we are getting $7,000,000 of paid-up stock which is liable to be worth a considerable amount by and by; that is the advantage which we are getting for the people of Canada. I say with reference to the action of Parliament last session, as I have said with reference to the proposed action this session, that aid to the Canadian Northern ought to be given entirely independent of and entirely irrespective of any transfer of common stock to the Government. The amendment which I propose, if adopted, will do away altogether with any idea of a .partnership. It will give the Government for a few years the control of this railway by means of the stock, which control may be exercised by active participation or otherwise as imav be deemed expedient from time to time. The position of creditor and debtor is retained. We say to the Canadian Northern Railway Company: We are willing to aid this enterprise, because we believe that it is to the advantage of the people of Canada that it should be carried to completion. iBut for a few years, until there lias been fully demonstrated your ability and the ability of the company to pay the charges which are against the property and to pay the interest upon the debentures amounting to $45,000,000 which the Government proposes to endorse for the Canadian Northern; until it is shown that you can meet promptly all the obligations which you engage to meet under this agreement, the whole stock of the company, the whole control of the company, shall remain in the hands of the Government. I think that is desirable, because in' ca^e there should be default the Government would be enabled at once, as the holder of the stock, to take steps for the purpose of exercising its right to control and of taking charge of the affairs of the company. The amendment which I propose provides for the holding of the stock for a period of five years. It provides also that the stock shall be reduced to $30,000,000. Today it is $77,000,000 and contains a great deal of water. It has not been shown to this House, and I do not for a

moment suppose that anybody believes it to foe true, that Mackenzie, Mann and Company have put any substantial amount of money into the undertaking. This vast sum of $77,000,000 is practically all watered stock. It may be said that it has been issued by authority of Parliament. It has not been in the sense in which Parliament declares stock to be paid up. That amount of stock, I grant you, has been authorized; but it has been paid up very largely by the manipulation of having Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, as contractors, and issuing, through their board of directors, the stock to them as fully paid up stock in consideration of their engaging to construct the various portions of the system. That is the way in which the stock very largely has been secured to be issued as fully paid up. But as to the actual payment of money into the enterprise in consideration of the issue of stock, so far as we know, so far as this Government have been able to tell us, so far as we believe, there was no substantial amount of cash* put into this undertaking to represent this capital stock. As I have already said, the whole idea-and I am not stopping now either to approve of it or to criticise it-of those gentlemen who have been promoting this railway has been that they would construct it without calling upon the capital stock; that they would lay that capital stock away in their own treasury and build the road out of the aid which would be given by the public in the way of money and land grants, and out of the proceeds of securities which the company might issue. It may be asked why do you name $30,000,000? There are two reasons why that should be done. The first reason is that the issued capital is $77,000,000. When the Government took the $7,000,000 at the last session, Parliament was assured that under ordinary circumstances the company would be able, with the amount of $16,000,000 which was then voted to the company, to complete the system without coming to the country for additional aid. But now it is proposed to add to the securities, and thereby add to the fixed charges, the enormous sum of $45,000,000. Capital is raised in two ways, by the issue of securities and by the issue of capital stock and now that it is proposed not to use the capital stock at all for the purpose of raising money to complete the system but to issue these securities to the amount of $45,000,000 to be en-
dorsed and guaranteed by the Government of the country, I say that tlhe, capital stock ought to be reduced to an amount equal at all events to the amount which is to be added to the charges upon the road which are secured by guarantee. If yon take $45,000,000, the amount of the charge which is now being created, from the issued stock of $77,000,000, it would reduce it down to $32,000,000. I have put it at $30,000,000. There is not a very great deal of difference because, after all, the question of the amount of capital stock is not very important, so far as Mackenzie, Mann and 'Company, Limited are concerned, or so far as the Government is concerned, except that in case the Government decided to take the road over, the amount Which the arbitrators would allow would be limited to the capital stock, and except in so far as it might influence the Board of Railway 'Commissioners in case an application were made to fix tolls, when undoubtedly they would have reference to the capital stock. But the difference, ae I have said, between $30,000,000 and $32,000,000 is not very great. I suggest that it should be made $30,000,000 for another reason, that there is nothing in the way of physical property of a value to represent anything more than $30,000,000. Nobody will contend that. This whole system, to a large extent, is being reorganized; the different companies are being consolidated as far as they can be consolidated and capital stock in the parent company is being issued. It ought to be for such an amount as will fairly represent the value of these properties over and above the securities or charges which are now standing against them. There is no man in this House who is familiar with the circumstances but will say that $30,000,000 is an ample amount at which to fix the capital stock, because it represents and more than represents the value of the equity of redemption of the company in this property.
You may ask what is the object of making a reduction. It is this, that in future, if the capital stock is at $100,000,000 which is almost entirely watered if not all watered, it would necessarily have its effect upon the Board of Railway Commissioners when they would come to determine what tolls should be allowed. That is an important consideration for the people of this country. More than that, if the capital stock is authorized by this Parliament at the enormous sum of $100,000,000, the investors to whom Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, may offer that stock would natur-

ally siippos-d that, in the opinion of this Parliament, it had a value behind it and that it ought to have a value in the markets of the world at least at all events approaching an equality to the value which Parliament put on it when it declared that it might be issued as fully paid up stock. Those are two reasons, I think, that ought to be regarded as sufficient and that is why I think it desirable to fix $30,000,000.
I am entirely opposed to the plan of the Government of increasing the capital stock. I have heard in the past quite a number of gentlemen on the other side of the House complain of the practice of companies issuing great quantities of common stock without any consideration, simply as watered stock. We know that Public Utilities Commissions have been appointed in the various provinces to make examination into the issue of stock by companies to prevent that practice. We know that stock is disposed of among innocent people for value, and they naturally expect a reasonable return upon the par value of the stock. I do not think I need argue this any further because it will appeal to every one as being reasonable that instead of increasing the stock it ought to be reduced down to a figure which is approximately representative of the actual value of the equity of redemption in these undertakings. The amendment provides that in case no default is made by the company in the payment of interest on the bonds to be guaranteed by His Majesty as provided in the resolution, and in case the conditions in the agreement in all other respects shall be carried out, then, at the end of the five years, this stock shall be returned to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. It will be borne in mind that included in the $30,000,000 which will go back to Mackenzie, Mann and Company under those circumstances is the $7,000,000 issued to the Government in pursuance of the legislation of last session. I think that it ought to go back. I think it was entirely indefensible for the Government to take it; it ought not to have influenced the Government or Parliament in their action in making the grant of $16,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
I think it ought to form part of the $30,000,000, and if Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or the Canadian Northern railway, which is the same thing, pay the interest upon these debentures and the charges upon the property, and if they carry out the agreement in all other respects for a period of five years I think that would test their ability to carry out the undertaking, and the $30,000,000 of stock might then be handed over to them subject, as the amendment provides, to the Government having the right at any time within the five years to take over the entire stock of the Canadian Northern and to become the entire owners of the Canadian Northern and its constituent and subsidiary companies subject to the encumbrances then existing against them. Does not my amendment propose to deal fairly with Mackenzie and Mann in the event of the road being taken over ? It provides that the value of the stock shall be fixed by arbitration, but that it shall not exceed the $30,000,000 which is to 'be the par value of the stock. It surprised me to hear the Solicitor General make the statement that my amendment if adopted' would lead at once to a receivership and to this company's going into bankruptcy. I was astonished at that remark. What does it mean, Sir? It means that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, who have been aided already by the people of this country to an amount exceeding $300,000,000-
That is only two and a half times too much.
How much is it then ?
Including land and subsidies.
Including everything the country has given to the Canadian Northern railway.
Including what the provinces have given ?
Yes.

My hon. friend may be right, but I was told differently. I will take my hon. friend's figures. The statement of my hon. friend is this: Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have gone into this enterprise as their own personal undertaking although under the name of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They come now to Parliament and ask for a $45,000,000 guarantee and they ask for that without putting up a dollar of their own 'security, and without telling Parliament what is the wealth of either of them to-day, or what is the wealth of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited; and that if Parliament were to say, we will grant your request but in granting it we make the condition that you shall be willing to have your stock reduced to $30,000,000 and the Government
43a6

shall have the right at any time within five years to take over that stock subject to all the liabilities which are now upwards of $300,000,000-my hon. friend will not contradict that-and we will pay you what arbitrators, mutually chosen, shall decide your stock is worth, but the amount shall not exceed $30,000,000, we will hand back the $7,000,000 of stock which you gave us last year, we will let that go into the pot-my hon. friend the Solicitor General tells this House that if that proposition were made to Mackenzie and Mann they would reject it with indignation and would allow this entire system to go into the hands of a receiver. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, may be masters of this Administration, but they are not the masters of the people of Canada, and if they were to say that to the Government I would say to Mackenzie and Mann: If you take that attitude, make default if you like upon your bonds and the Government of Canada will immediately take steps to enter into possession under the securities which we have guaranteed, and the different provinces can be trusted to do the same thing. I am inclined to think it might not be a very bad thing for this country if that position were taken towards Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. According to the argument of my hon. friend, the more deeply Mackenzie and Mann get the country involved the stronger argument they can make to Parliament because they can terrify Parliament and the Government, according to my hon. friend, by the threat that they will lie down and let the country do the best it can with the property which they have created through public aid. I do not believe that Mackenzie and Mann would take that attitude. I believe that if any one were to offer them $15,000,000 apiece in cash for their equity of redemption in this property they would gladly take it. At all events, if they would not take it they would be bigger fools than I imagine them to be.
Would the hon. gentleman recommend that the Government make that offer now?

Not to-d'ay, no, because the people of Canada have not authorized.* this Parliament to commit them to government ownership of the Canadian Northern system. I do not ask Parliament to give power to the Government to take over the road, but what I say is that the idea of government ownership and operation of a transcontinental railway system is growing, and, I believe, growing rapidly in this

country. If my amendment were to carry, no doubt the matter would be discussed in the public press and from the public platforms of this country, and after the next election we should know very well the views of the people of Canada on government ownership. Strong argument could be made from the fact that we have in eastern Canada a government-owned and operated system, and that we have in the West, extending from the Saskatchewan river up to Hudson bay, a government road which will be some 500 miles in length. The people might very w*ell say that it is desirable in the public interest that this system should be extended from the Atlantic to the Pacific. ,1 do not propose to bind the Government or Parliament upon the question of government ownership, but, as Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann admit to-day that they are in a helpless condition, and that, although this is the fourth time within the last four years they have come to this Parliament for aid, yet they must come, and that, unless the Government guarantees their bonds to the extent of $45,000,000, they will not be able to finish the undertaking, I say that under those circumstances it would be doing no injustice to Mackenzie and Mann to say: We are willing to guarantee your bonds, but you must give us an option on your equity of redemption in the road, in order that if, at any time within five years, the people of this country should consider it desirable to take over the road, they may-do so at a price to be fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed the amount of $30,000,000. Tf this enterprise is a failure the Government will be called upon to take over the entire system. We hope it will not be a failure. I have the greatest possible confidence in this country, and more particularly in the West. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that it was practically only in 1900, some four years after the Liberal party came into power, that the West began to develop, and that tihe people of the world began to realize the resources of our western country. .It is a remarkable fact that that knowledge was first brought home by immigrants who came in from the country to the south of us. It was then that they first discovered the richness of the great province of Saskatchewan and they began to come into Canada by hundreds and thousands and tens of thousands. That province, or at all events a great portion of it, that for a century or more had been looked upon as

being the northern extension of the great American desert, was discovered to be land of the greatest possible fertility and that land which was thought to be a desert is regarded to-day as being the very garden of the Northwest. So it is with the other Western provinces; business began to increase in 1900, and they developed rapidly from that time on. What has been the history of the Canadian Pacific railway? In 1900, although that road had been in operation for fifteen years right across the continent, its total gross earnings were only $36,000,000; in the short period of thirteen years its earnings have grown from $36,000,000 to $130,000,000 or nearly 400 per cent. 'That shows you what the country is capable of.
I have the greatest possible hope that, the present period of depression will speedily pass away, that immigrants will again begin to come into this country in as great number as before, that business upon the Canadian Northern railway will revive, and that before very many years it will be a success. But what is to make it a success? It is because this Government is pledging the credit of the people of Canada to an amount of $45,000,000. Is it not reasonable that in asking the Government to do this, in asking them to put upon a sound basis an undertaking which to-day is bankrupt, the company should be willing to say to the Government: in consideration of your doing this, we will grant to you an option, which you may exercise at any time within five years from this date, to take over the property at a fair and reasonable valuation to be fixed by arbitration. I do not think that if that proposition were made to Mackenzie, Mann and Company they would reject it. I do not think they would dare to reject it. I cannot imagine that they made that threat to my hon. friend or to the Government and I rather think it is just simply a voluntary statement on my hon. friend's part intended to influence the House against the amendment that I am proposing.
I perhaps ought to explain in regard to the provision I am making in the amendment, with reference to the $25,000,000 of income charge convertible debenture stock. The House will remember that it has been stated that there is an issue of $25,000,000 of income charge debenture stock, the holders of which have the right, on notice to the company, to convert that stock into $25,000,000 of common stock at par value. I do not think there will be any likelihood
in the near future of that right being exercised, but still, suppose Parliament were to have the good judgment to act upon the suggestion which I humbly venture to submit to the House and accept my amendment, provision would have to be made for the issuing of this $25,000,000 of stock in order to keep faith with the holders of the income charge convertible debenture stock in case they should decide to exercise the option. That is the only reason why I have made reference to it in the amendment.
I am not going to detain the House because I realize that the matter has been thoroughly threshed out and that the House would like to come to the decision of the various questions which may be raised by amendment, as speedily as possible. I thought it desirable to explain what is intended by the amendment. I just wish to say one word in answer to my hon. friend the Solicitor General, who took occasion to mention my name when he was addressing the House before recess. He said that we complained because the Canadian Northern townsite of Mount Royal, at Montreal, had not been included in the securities which the Government propose to take. Then he said:	How
inconsistent the Opposition are; at one time they say that the Government should not speculate in the stock of the Canadian Northern, and then they want us to' speculate in Canadian Northern townsites. My hon. friend did not do himself justice when he made that remark,	particularly in	view	of	thefact that he	made a strong	point	to	theHouse that we were getting security upon the equity of redemption in the common stock of the Canadian Northern Town Properties Company, whose whole property consists of interests in townsites, who have no other assets, no other property, the security upon which my hon. friend thought it of such importance for the Government to take that	he devoted a special	clauseto it, which	clause will be	found	in	the
resolution. There is the difference between the hon. gentleman and those of us who have been discussing this matter from our standpoint. The hon. gentleman seems to have taken for the Government just those townsites which Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, chose to give him, and those are the townsites which to-day are of the least value, but when it comes to the great, and the most valuable, townsite in what will be the heart of the city of Montreal,

in the favourite residential part of Montreal, the hon. gentleman says: oh, do not find fault with us for leaving that out, because that would be speculating in town-sites.

Because they do not
own it.

That is not the argument that the hon. gentleman made yesterday. The argument that the horn. gentleman made yesterday was that we should not speculate in townsites. The hon. gentleman thinks it all right to speculate in town-sites that are of little value-townsites in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-

speechtext: Port Mann, for instance.

I am told that they
have milked Port Mann pretty well. The Government ought to have taken security upon all the new (town-sites in British Columbia. We do know that quite recently the Grand Trunk Pacific put Prince George on the market and they are said to have realized $3,000,000 from that one townsite alone. But as my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) says, Port Mann was milked pretty well by Mackenzie, Mann and Company before they venture to offer it to the Government. Let us take for a moment the townsite at Montreal. The hon. the Solicitor General says that the Canadian Northern does not own it. I know, iand everybody else in Montreal knows, that when it was proposed to run the tunnel through Mount Royal, it WU3 recognized that it would bring all of that district upon the northern side of the mountain within five minutes of the business portion of the city. The land is beautifully situated. It was announced in the newspapers that a gentleman from Winnipeg, under the direction of Messrs. Davidson, MoCrea. and Company, who handle all the townsites and all the land of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, would come to Montreal to take charge of it. Messrs. Davidson, MoCrae and Company opened their offices in Montreal and sold the land as being the land of the Canadian Northern. It is splendidly situated just in the vicinity of where the railway will enter the tunnel under Mount Royal. I venture to say that that townsite is worth $20,000,000.
I repeat that it is worth $20,000,000. I venture to say that they have taken or will take that much money out of it. Let me

ask you, Mr. -Speaker, whether, if Mackenzie, Mann and 'Company, Limited, -have put the proceeds of that townsite into the pockets of themselves and their associates instead of into the Canadian Northern Railway Company, that is playing fair with the people of this country? These townsites are made valuable by the railway. What would Fort George townsite be worth but for the Grand Trunk Pacific railway? What would this townsite north of Mount Royal at Montreal be worth but for the Canadian Northern railway? It would be valuable for very little more than simply farm lands. Yet by reason of the Canadian Northern building this tunnel through the mountain, thus bringing all this district within five minutes of the /business centre of the city of Montreal, this townsite has been made of this enormous value. The only inference, however, to be drawn from the remarks of my hon. friend, taken in connection with the fact well known to the people of Montreal that this townsite is handled as a Canadian Northern townsite, is that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have not put it into the hands of the Can-dian Northern but have kept in their own hands what should have /been the interest of the railway. That matter ought to be investigated. My hon. friend says the member for St. John ought to give us the information about it. I am not in touch with Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. The hon. gentleman is.; he has been for weeks, perhaps for months, in consultation with Mr. Lash, solicitor for the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

My hon. friend misinterprets me. I have given the information. The result of my investigation is that they do not own the townsite. My hon. friend contradicts that statement. If he wishes, he can endeavour to establish his contention. If he establishes his contention in goes the townsite.

Does my hon. friend
say that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, do not own the townsite?
They do not own it. I have said so four or five times.

And does he say that
they have not the larger part of the stock of the company in whose name the townsite is?

I will make a further statement along that line. I have already said that they do not own it, and I can say

to the hon. gentleman now that their interest, in whatever shape it may be, is a fractional one and is purely speculative, and one into which, I think, having regard to the professed principles of hon. gentlemen opposite, it would be heresy itself to lead this country.
The hon. gentleman is apparently able to get some information.
I have given the hon. gentleman that information several times.

No; the hon. gentleman has only told us now that that is the interest they have. What would be thought of Sir Thomas Shaughnessy and Mr. David Mc-Nicoll if, as they built railways in various sections of Canada, they looked out ahead and got the titles to the townsites in their own names or in the names of companies which they controlled, and did not let the townsites stand in the name of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? As a matter of fact, in the West, the townsites which are created by the Canadian Pacific railway are sold and disposed of by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have adopted a different course, because I find that in the trust deed to the British Empire Trust Company all these townsites in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the town-site of Port Mann in British Columbia, have been declared to be the property of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. My own judgment is that my hon. friend, knowing how very valuable is this Mount Royal townsite, being able to learn, as he should be, from the slightest inquiry that it was put on the market as a Canadian Northern townsite, ought to have made the further inquiry and to have found out what was the interest of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, in that townsite.
I will not detain the House further. I submit this amendment to the judgment of the House. I hope that it will meet with the approval of the majority of the members of this House; but whether it meets with their approval or not, I am satisfied that it will meet with the approval of the majority of the people of this country.
