speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Pu,gsley) has gone in some detail into the whole question, which has been debated at very great length already in this House. I do not think I need follow him in like detail, and therefore I will confine myself to the main points put forward by him in favour of his amendment.
In the first place, my hon. friend, who has a policy of his own on this question, like a great many of the hon. members opposite, seems to have framed this amendment in such a way that it has the quality of fluidity in a remarkable degTee.
What is that word?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Fluidity; it has the quality of fluidity: it changes its form very rapidly. Two days ago my hon. friend gave notice of a motion which contained this clause:
To provide that until default is made in the payment of interest or in the carrying out ofl other provisions of said resolution and agreement, or until the Governor in Council exercises such option, the nominees of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, shall he the directors of the company, and be in control of its affairs.
That portion of the proposed amendment has been dropped. Thus the motion of which my hon. friend gave notice two days ago differs from that which he moved to-day in an exceedingly important respect. In the one case, Mackenzie and Mann, through their nominees, were to have control of this road until default should occur, or until the Governor in Council should exercise the option provided for in the resolution. In the amendment he now proposes, he has entirely omitted that provision. He undertakes to explain that omission, and the substance of bis explanation, so far as I could follow him, is, that he thinks the resolution should be in its present form because it is different from that which he at first proposed.
I think the hon. gentleman was not following me very closely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that however,
closely one may follow the hon. gentleman he will receive no other impression from his speech. It is a fortunate thing that this debate was not postponed until tomorrow for by that time the resolution would probably have assumed another form, and we do not know what amendment he might have been then inclined to put forward.
This amendment in its present form means if it means anything, that the Government of Canada should undertake the completion and operation of a road which they do not own and may never own. I do not know whether my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition is sufficiently rapid to keep up with the political gyrations of the hon. member for St. John, but he will have to take many and long steps

if he is fo keep the pace with him in this matter. In 1904, the question of public ownership was considerably discussed in this House, and we moved a resolution declaring that as the people of Canada were providing about nine-tenths of the cash and credit required for the construction of the National Transcontinental railway, it would be better to provide the other tenth' and own the whole line from Moncton to Prince Rupert. The right hon. gentleman scoffed at the idea of extending the principle of government ownership and operation of railways. He told us that he had gone with Mr. J .R. Booth, I think it was, to Parry Sound, had looked out upon the waters of the Georgian bay and had seen the Canada Atlantic steamers there and had made himself acquainted with all the complexities -and developments connected with the operation of a modern railway system and had come to the conclusion that such considerations forbade the Government from embarking upon any policy of state ownership of railways. He is reported in ' Hansard ' of 1904, at 5 p.m. page 1646 as speaking in defence of the National Transcontinental Railway proposals and in opposition to the proposal we advocated. After giving considerable attention to the subject, he said:
That is the reason we thought it preferable to adopt the plan we have adopted rather than go into government ownership which seems to be a fad that is rather developing on the other side of the House.
And in the campaign literature which the right hon. gentleman circulated in the general election of 1904 in defence of the National Transcontinental proposal appeared the following:
Some persons in this country are frequently told that because the State aids the railways it should own them, and to the public mind this includes the operation of them by the Government. If any one of the various railway policies contrived by Mr. R. L. Borden means the extension of the Intercolonial railway across the continent, operated as a public work, then the Government of Canada takes issue with Mr. Borden, and says that it does not believe it would be in the public interest to operate the Grand Trunk Pacific as a government work.
That was the position of my right hon. friend in 1904, and that is the position, so far as I understand it, that he has taken ever since. It has remained for the hon. member for St. John to pull forward- rather reluctantly I should judge-the right hon. leader of the Opposition into a policy

which goes much further than anything we proposed in 1904. For, while the policy proposed by the hon. member for St. John might conceivably result in the ownership of this railway system, it does contemplate and distinctly provide for the operation by the Government of a great transcontinental line of railway before the Government has any ownership in that line. That is pushing the theory of state operation a little further than it has ever been pushed in this country or in any other. Whatever may be the merits or demerits of state ownership and operation of railways I should think it would be a fairly reasonable proposition that it will be quite time enough for the Government to undertake the operation of a great transcontinental line when it has acquired the ownership of that line.
Then, what does the hon. gentleman propose further? He proposes that the proprietary interest of the capital stock of this railway shall be cut down to $30,000,000. I do not know whether he means that the stock is to be taken compulsorily or by agreement. Does he suggest that we shall confiscate the stock, or does he suggest that we shall negotiate?

I suggest that it be
made a part of the agreement under which we give this guarantee, that that shall be a condition and that they shall consent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And if they will not consent, he thinks we should permit the road to go into a receivership?
Mi- PUGSLEY: That is another matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let me show how far that squares with what has been done in other cases. In 1904, the Government of which the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was the leader authorized the capitalization of $45,000,000 for a little over 1,700 miles of railway from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. The capitalization of the Canadian Northern railway, under the present arrangement, cannot be increased beyond $100,000,000 without the consent of Parliament, and when it is completed it will comprise nearly 10,000 miles of railway. The authorized capitalization of the Grand Trunk Pacific on the same basis would be nearly $250,000,000. Or, if you take the issued stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, $25,000,000, the capitalization of the Canadian Northern railway on that basis would be $130,000,000 or $135,000,000. My hon. friend speaks of this stock as ' watered stock.' He says that Mackenzie and Mann have never put a dol-

lar into this road. We have shown in this House over and over again that they have put in nearly $30,000,000 of lands to which they had as good a title as has the hon. gentleman to any of his holdings in the West. We have shown that they put in the security of townsites, and the assets of other companies that they have organized. More than that, they have put into this enterprise lands at Port Arthur which they acquired at a very low price in its early stages, and they have put these lands in at those low prices for which they were bought many years ago. There are computations which they have submitted to us, but with which I have not thought it worth while to weary the House, and which show, that at least >$40,000,003 or $50,000,000 of assets made up in this way have gone into this road. And he calls this ' watered stock.' Let us see about the stock authorized by his leader under an agreement which, I presume, he supported in 1904. The Grand Trunk Pacific was authorized to issue $25,000,000 of common stock, and it was provided that the Grand Trunk railway should hold that stock. It was authorized to issue also $20,000,000 of preferred stock. I believe that the preferred stock has not been issued up to the present time. And what we said would happen in the case of the common stock is what actually happened,-the Grand Trunk Pacific, being authorized by this Government under an arrangement made between that company and this Government, handed that stock over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company without the payment of one single dollar. In consideration of what? In consideration of the Grand Trunk Railway Company guaranteeing a certain portion, about one-quarter of the securities upon, the mountain section and all the securities beyond $13,000 a nude on the prairie section. This country, which guaranteed three-fourths of the securities upon the mountain section and undertook to implement those secur- . ities, to pay interest upon them for seven years without recourse and to lease the eastern division to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for seven years without any rental, received not one single dollar of consideration for the guaranteeing of those securities. I would like to ask my hon. friend whether or not he considers that the $25,000,000 of .stock handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company under the agreement made by his leader and supported by himself in 1903-04 was watered stock?

I am informed by a
gentleman who should know, because he is an officer of the company, that the Grand Trunk railway, in consideration of that agreed to guarantee the bonds, and that they actually guaranteed upwards of $40,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The country, which has
already guaranteed $70,000,000 in oin.e mortgage and which has also loaned money to this company, did not receive any compensation of that kind. If. my hon. friend thinks that the guarantee of $40,000,000 was ample compensation, sufficient to make the stock fuLly paid up, what does he think of this stock, inasmuch as the present proprietors have put in lands of the vailue of nearly $30,000,000 and, besides that, have financed the construction of this road for eighteen years, from the time it was first commenced, placing their personal and individual credit at the command of this company for that purpose during all these years? In the construction, of a railway which costs over $350,000,000, it must be obvious to every man in this House that a very large amount of working .construction capital must be provided. Some one must either provide that money or make himself liable for it. I would ask the hon. member for the city of St. John if he believes for one moment that during that period of eighteen years these gentlemen, have not made themselves liable first and last for at least the amount which he has mentioned? They have, and, in addition to that, they have put in lands worth thirty million dollars, which they- held as their own property by a title that vas absolutely good under the law. Taking all these things into consideration, I leave it to the judgment of every hon. gentleman in this House as to whether or not the term watered stock can be best applied to the stock of the Canadian Northern railway or to the stock of the company to which I have just now alluded. I do not think there can be any difference of opinion on the subject. We all know that in this country railway stock has been issued on a great many occasions without actual payment in cash, but so far [DOT] as this stock is concerned assets of very large and substantial amounts were put into the concern as consideration for that stock.
Then in addition to what I have said, we called upon this company, upon Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and upon Sir

William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, to release every possible claim they had for all agency services and commission extending over a period of eighteen years in respect of the construction of the road during all these years; and, further, to release profits, if there were any, that they could have charged in respect of the construction of the road.
My hon. friend has said that we are greatly to iblame because certain townsites are not given to the Government as security. I have not recently refreshed my recollection, but I have a distinct impression that in 1909, when the loan of $10,000,000 was made, we, the Conservative Opposition, made a motion that the townsites in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company should be brought in as security to the country in respect of the guarantee then proposed to be made. In this instance we put in town-sites to the number of nearly 300. My hon. friend says that others should have been put in, but we put in every townsite that, so far as we could understand, bad any connection with the road. The one to which attention was called by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, Port Mann, was put in and forms part of the security, for whatever value there is in it. My hon. friend says that we are not playing fair with the people of the country because other townsites have not been brought in as part of the security. He knows how many have been included; if he can satisfy us upon any reasonable evidence that there are any others which should be brought in, we shall be glad to insist that they be included, but I do not propose to take into consideration in connection with that, mere street rumour, or such expressions as ' it is said ' or ' I am told.' Action by Parliament requires to be based upon something more than that, and up to the present time my hon. friend has given us nothing more.
My hon. friend says that he does not make his proposal with a view to government ownership or government operation at the present time; that that subject may be discussed at the next general election. I think my hon. friend has really given the key to his motion. He does not intend that this amendment shall be taken seriously, but he does desire to have something to talk about at the next general election.
I should like to see it passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend and his friends are very wonderful in one respect.

When they are in opposition they are ready to destroy any supposed evil; their zeal knows no bounds; they profess to be ready to tear it to pieces. Whether it be protection, trusts or combines, or anything else, just let them get at it; let them have the reins of power and these injustices will be destroyed at the earliest possible moment. But when they attain power, they roar as gently as any sucking dove. In 1896 they came into power; how long was it before they destroyed protection? Just before they went out of power, they were arm in arm with protection, as they were, indeed, all through their term of office. So in regard to these corporations. My hon. friends sitting in opposition on the other side of the House, are ready to spring upon any corporation, take it by the throat, shake it, make it yield up its stock, destroy it, if necessary; have no mercy upon it. But, when they come into power we find them closeted with corporations, linked up with them in every possible way, and treating them as gently as it would be possible to treat their dearest friends. So it has been in this case, because, if I am not mistaken, there was no such particular antipathy to the Canadian Northern railway, or to any person associated with that railway, in 1911, when it came here and got a guarantee of $35,000,000. If I am not mistaken, my hon. friends opposite were very good friends with these supposed buccaneers, very good friends, indeed. I do not think any hon. gentleman opposite will deny that statement; I do not think any of them would have the hardihood to do it. Mackenzie and Mann at that time were enterprising, patriotic, pure-minded Canadians, to whom the country owed a great debt of gratitude; to-day they are buccaneers. And yet, if these hon. gentlemen came into power to-morrow, they would undergo a rapid change of heart. Indeed, I think distinguished honours conferred on these gentlemen were conferred at the instance of my right hon. friend. I really am astonished that he should have it in mind to advise the conferring of honours of that kind by the Crown upon gentlemen who have been described by some of his friends as of such doubtful character. When did these hon. gentlemen opposite discover that these men were buccaneers? It is greatly to be regretted that they did not make some investigation in 1911 and make the discovery at that time. We know that all this commotion does not accurately express the state of mind of

hon. gentlemen opposite. We realize that perfeetly well, and we realize that any one of them, my hon. friend from St. John in particular, may think it desirable to play what he imagines is a profitable political game; hut I hope he will not expect that anyone, either in this House or in the country, will take the playing of that game very seriously. The people understand their motive.
The whole situation, so far as we are concerned, is this: The late Administration, in 1903 and 1904, conceived the idea of building another transcontinental railway, and they said that time would not wait, that they were impelled to undertake it at once. Later on, indeed I think in that very session of 1904, they acknowledged that the Canadian Northern railway had the status of a transcontinental railway, and in 1911 they formally stated that fact in the recital to an Act of Parliament, and gave that company aid by guarantee to the extent of $35,000,000. They thus undertook the project of building two additional transcontinental railroad S' in this country when it had a population of little more than 7,000,000. That was a very great task for a population of that number to assume. My right hon. friend gave up the reins of office, and we had to assume them. We were confronted with the prospect that the construction of this transcontinental railway would be stopped and indefinitely delayed. The situation was by no means .an easy situation, and we solved it in this way: We said, in the first place, that, so far as the Canadian Northern railway and its allied -companies were concerned, their capital must be reduced. My hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) thinks that by repeating the statement, successfully controverted, over and over again, that the capital stock has been increased, he may impress some person with the idea that there is something in his assertion. Let me tell him that to-day, before this agreement is consummated, Mackenzie and Mann own $i0,-000,000 stock in the Canadian Northern railway, and $68,000,000 of stock in the allied companies. When this Bill is passed and this agreement is consummated, Mackenzie and Mann will not own either $70,000,000 or $138,000,000, they will own $60,000,000 of stock, or $78,000,000 less stock than they owned originally. They Had $138,000,000, that is the $70,000,000, in the Canadian Northern railway and the $68,000,000 in the subsidiary companies; we had
$7,000,000 of stock in the Canadian Northern railway and no more. After the agreement is consummated Mackenzie and Mann will have but $60,000,000 in the Canadian Northern railway and the Government of Canada will have $40,000,000 in the Canadian Northern railway.
It has been demonstrated over and over again to the satisfaction of every member in this House that by the method which we have taken the capital stock of that system is effectually and absolutely reduced to $100,000,000 and no more. Further than that, we have provided that it cannot be increased without the consent of Parliament. Under these circumstances it seems to me that there is no good reason whatever for the proposal of my hon. friend. We guarantee $45,000,000 for the completion of this road. The Government of Canada will make that guarantee under such conditions as will ensure that every dollar raised out of the proceeds of those securities will go into that road and after it has gone into that road we will have a two-fifths interest in all the advantages that may come out of the future success of the enterprise. In marked contrast in that respect is our proposal to any proposal- ever brought forward by hon. gentlemen opposite.
My hon. friend from St. John speaks of partnership and that cry has been repeated by almost every member on the other side who has spoken. The hon. gentleman from St. John knows as well as I do that there i& no partnership, otherwise he would have to contend that every man of the 30,000 shareholders of the Canadian Pacific railway is in partnership with every other one of those shareholders. Does he mean to contend that? I would not think he would be guilty of that absurdity, and I am glad to see he is not. But if that be not true, then it is not true that the Government of Canada is in partnership with Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, or any one else. The truth is that the Government of Canada has, by means of its assumption of this portion of the stock issue, acquired an interest in the road and in all successes and advantages which may come to it in the future; and in that regard I am sure that the people of Canada will approve of the action of this Government.
I was speaking of the situation we had to face. We had to assure the completion of this transcontinental railway and not to allow any collapse; not to allow the credit of this country to be endangered in financial markets abroad; not to allow thousands of people in this country to suffer from the

certain results of any collapse of this enterprise. What did we insist upon? We insisted that the stock should be reduced to $100,000,000 and that the companies, I think some thirty in number, comprising this system should be amalgamated so far as it was possible to amalgamate them and that the road should be brought under one management. We felt that, if the people of Canada lent their credit to the completion of this enterprise, then the people of Canada'were reasonably entitled to participate to a large etxent in its future success. I have no fear at all of the judgment which the people of Canada will pass upon the action of the Government. We have made, in respect of the aid which we now bring to insure the completion of this road, an infinitely better bargain than any of the same character ever made by my hon. friends on the other side of the House. We are absolutely prepared to meet hon. gentlemen opposite, on this question before the electorate of Canada, when the proper time comes.

Inasmuch as the question of public ownership has come up in this discussion, I propose to refer to it for just a few moments, and also to the amendment of the hon. member for St. John. I agree with what the Prime Minister has just said, that it was the duty of Parliament and the Government to come to the aid of the Canadian Northern railway because of the action of the previous Government and of the previous Parliament, and also because if they had refused to accept responsibility in this matter the credit of Canada would have been greatly injured and there might have been a panic in this country. In coming to the aid of this concern, the Government has done something that the public will approve of, and which they were more or less compelled to do to save some of the provinces who had been too free with their credit in encouraging unnecessary duplicate transcontinental lines when they could better have employed their money in building local railways. Be that as it may, the credit of the country had to be maintained and the responsibility was on the Government, and to my mind the proposition before the House is pretty nearly the only possible proposition under the circumstances. Further, the Canadian Northern railway is a great transcontinental system. It will have the best grades of any of the three transcontinental systems in this country. Its feeder lines are, I believe, the equal of the Canadian Pacific railway, and

better than those of the Grand Trunk Pacific. It has every prospect of being a first-class transcontinental line, and it has also the facility of developing traffic. It is surprising the way the Canadian Northern railway, in its short career, has developed traffic from one end of the country to the other. I regard that road as a very valuable transcontinental proposition, and above all it is the one transcontinental road that ought to fit in and join up with our present public owned railway, the Intercolonial railway. I absolutely believe in public ownership in regard to these great propositions. Every time I have been returned to this House I have been pledged to my supporters to uphold the principle of public ownership. If the people of South York and of the city of Toronto believe in anything it is in public ownership, and when I speak in favour of public ownership I speak not only for myself but for my constituency, for my neighbours, for my city, and I believe I speak for the great province of Ontario. We to-day in the province of Ontario believe in public ownership absolutely. We have a Government in Ontario to-day that has the confidence of the people of Ontario more than any previous Government, for the reason that it believes in public ownership and is applying that principle to-day to local radial lines to be linked up with the greater systems. The other day a deputation from Ontario came to this Government-and it was the finest deputation I ever saw here, of men from all counties and cities in Ontario and of both political parties-to say that the people of Ontario absolutely believe in the principle of public ownership as applied to the railways of Ontario, and, inferentially, a wider application of the principle. We have a press in Ontario that is largely in favour of public ownership, and we have in this House men who believe in public ownership and who are here to uphold that doctrine. The people in the Maritime provinces already have public ownership and the people of the West are believing in it more and more, and the whole tendency of this country is in the direction of public ownership of at least one transcontinental railway linked up with the Intercolonial. As one who believes in public ownership, I would like to see something in this agreement that would provide for the acquisition of the Canadian Northern by the people of this country. I think that could be done in absolute harmony with the agreement, but it could not be done on the lines suggested

by the hon. member for St. John as it would involve the breaking of the agreement, as the Prime Minister has just pointed out. The agreement has to be carried out practically as it is, but is it not possible to so modify it as to ultimately secure public ownership of this system?

The agreement is not
executed yet; it is still open.

Yes, it is still open.
Now we come to Mackenzie -and Mann. I know both these gentlemen very well and have known them for a long while. I have listened to a great deal of criticism passed upon them in this House, perhaps some of it justly, and I have often criticised them myself both in this House -and outside, but I have this to say: Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are the first men I have met connected with the railroads or public utilities of this country who are ready to sell out to the public under fair terms. The Mayor of Toronto has been negotiating with Sir William Mackenzie for the purchase by the city of the Toronto Street railway and the Toronto Electric Light Company, and Sir William Mackenzie is willing to sell out on what I consider fair terms. I believe he once offered to sell out his franchise in the city of Winnipeg.
What is the price for the Toronto Street railway?

It has not been definitely fixed, but is about $20,000,000, and if the matter comes up -again I am going to argue that it would be a good proposition for the city of Toronto to buy the Street railway and the Electric Light Company for $20,000,000, or something in that neighbourhood. I think it is well , known, as the Prime Minister said just now, that the Mackenzie interests are not only willing to sell out their Street railway franchises, but also their radial lines in the province of Ontario, and their transmission lines and the generating plant in connection with the development of power at Niagara Falls.

Why do they not sell
the Toronto Street railway?

One reason given was
that Sir William was fully occupied with tue proposition now before the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
rather wandering away from the question beiore the House.

I am discussing public ownership and I wish to confine myself to the amendment of the hon. member for St. Jonn which has that principle in view. All I have to say is that these men are willing to sell out their interests to the public, perhaps at a reasonable price. If that is the case my suggestion to the hon. member for St. John is this: Leave the resolutions as they are -and drop everything in his amendment but the last -clause which I will! read to the House.
The bon. gentleman referred to the Toronto Street railway as being worth $20,000,000. Does that represent its total value? Is it not a fact that Sir William Mackenzie owns only a small portion of it?
H-e has the management only.
The Mackenzie interest has only a small portion of it?

Yes, but he acted as the authority for the company to sell it completely, and also for the company controlling the electric light system. The whole franchise would be cancelled and turned over to the public.
I ask this question because the impression might go out that Sir William Mackenzie had $20,000,000 in it.
No, the stock is much less than that. They got the whole property. The hon. member for Charlevoix (Sir R. Forget) may know more about the details than I do.

He has the control?
Mr. MAC-LEAN: Yes, he has a sufficient interest to enable him to make the proposition. Inasmuch as the people of Canada are coming to the relief of the Canadian Northern railway, and therefore should acquire it, I believe there ought to be a clause in the agreement on the lines of the .last paragraph in the proposed amendment of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). Therefore, I would like to see it read in this way, and if we make this change perhaps there are a good many members who will vote for it:
(a) To provide that the Governor in Council shall have the option at any time, within a period of five years, to acquire the absolute ownership of the $60,000,000 of stock remaining outside of the $40,000,000 stock held for His Majesty, making up the $100,000,000 as described in section 12 of the resolution, and of the said Canadian Northern Railway System,



and of all the constituent and subsidiary companies mentioned in the said resolution or proposed agreement, subject to existing ijn-cumbrances, and to arrangements regarding-the conversion of the income charge convertible debenture stock, for a price to be fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed the sum of $30,000,000.

T.hat is better than nothing.
'Mr. MA'CLEiAtN:	That is better tihan
nothing. When we are making a bargain with this company, putting the credit of Canada behind it and burdening ourselves with this debt, we ought to have an option on that $'60,000,000 of stock remaining. I would not consider $30,000,000 as an excessive value for that stock. I do not know what the views of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, who own that stock, may be in regard to the matter, but I believe that they would be willing to negotiate with the Government now, in view of their being prepared to sell their other interests, and that they would be prepared to give an option on that remaining $00,000,000. We ought to get 5* now and not leave it to the future. At the present time it would be a cheap investment. There has been money put into this great transcontinental railway by that firm. It is a most valuable line, and it is worth the money. It will help to build up this country, and this railway links up with the Intercolonial better than any system we have. If we secured that option the people of Canada would endorse it, and I believe that the people expect us to obtain it. If the amendment is changed in the way I suggest it will not interfere with the resolution in any respect. It makes provision for the completion of the road, but in return for the guarantees that we are giving, and for what we are doing for the company, we ought to have an option on the railway.
We never can get control of the Canadian Pacific railway unless we buy its stock, but its capital to-day is $300,000,000 and the . stock is valued at double that amount. The greatest crime against the people of Canada with reference to the Canadian Pacific railway was the unstatesmanlike policy of allowing it to increase its capital stock. When I came into this House the Canadian Pacific railway had only a capital stock of $60,000,000 or less than that. It has been greatly increased. When we allowed it to be increased up to the enormous sum at which it stands to-day, we lost the opportunity of getting possession of the road except at an enormous cost. We should have
[Mr. W. P. Maclean.!
got control of the stock at the point at which it then stood, we should have forced them to finance through the issue of bonds, and then, for a comparatively few millions, we could have got control of the road at any time.
Here is a company with a smaller capitalization. The capital stock is being reduced to $100,000,000.. We have $40,000,000 of it; they have $60,000,000, and I believe that we ought to be able to get an option on this $60,000,000. If we do that we will make provision for public ownership. There has been a great deal of talk about public ownership, and all of us have taken more or less refuge in it in order to meet the conditions that have arisen. The people of Canada believe in public ownership and the people of the United States are coming to believe in it. I believe in it. The hon. gentleman said that after the next election there might be a party which would be in favour of public ownership. I hope to see a party in the next election in favour of public ownership, and I am going to associate myself in the next election with the men who believe in the principle of public ownership.
Would it not be a good thing to allow somebody to try this out, and then if it is all right we can take it over ?
It has been tried out all over and it has succeeded. Public ownership has succeeded everywhere that it has been tried.
What about the Intercolonial ?

Public ownership must be administered by men who believe in it, and must be supported by .a parliament tnat believes in it. The people of Canada do believe in it and they are going to return a parliament that believes in it. When we have such a parliament as that 1 will not be afraid of public ownership. We are not afraid of it in Ontario to-day. It has proved a great success in connection with the Hydro-electric, and in connection with the portion of the street railway in Toronto which the people own. We are not afraid of it in Ontario, we believe in the principle, and wherever the men administering it believe in it success results. 1 am not going to be judged on the question of public ownership under the administration of men who do not believe in it, and I .am not going to take any great stock in men who say they are public ownership

men and who do not live up to their principles.
I want to give an incident to prove how this principle is spreading in this country. The people are demanding it. We had the Liberal party in office, we have the present Conservative party in office, and a number of the members of these parties have professed to be public ownership men. I will tell you how you can test out the question as to the attitude of the two parties. Has there been a single public ownership man appointed to the Senate? What man can profess public ownership, or profess to be friendly to it, and be in a position to recommend or suggest the name of a man for appointment to the Senate? We hear professions in this House, we hear talk in all directions in favour of public ownership and we either believe in it or we do not. I believe in it, my constituents believe in it, and the great majority of the people of Ontario believe in it, We are going into a campaign in Ontario to acquire from Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited-and I hope it will come out in the forthcoming elections that ihe people of Ontario are prepared to carry out this project-their transmission lines, their radial lines and the generating plant in connection with the development of power in the province of Ontario, we are to begin a new policy of local radial railways for the development of this province. Here is a great opportunity in connection with the proposal now before the House to have the principle of public ownership injected into this proposition without in any way counteracting the resolutions. While I cannot vote for the hon. gentleman's amendment, I make the suggestion that, if the Government' can see its way to amend this proposition- I do not say that $30,000,000 is a fair price; perhaps the owners will say it is not, but let the maximum price be put into this agreement-the Government should make this amendment and then, at any time when it appears to the Government and to the Parliament of this country desirable to try the principle of public ownership, they will be free to do so. There is no cure for the railway grievances of this country except the competition of a public-owned line as against the private-owned corporations. We have not been able to bring the public-owned corporations to time by means of the Railway Commission, but we shall be able to regulate this line. That being the case, and if the proposition now before the House is not damaged 'by this suggestion of mine, why not carry it out and put this country 278$
in a position of being able to acquire a transcontinental line any day after this agreement is concluded? If we leave the proposition until the question of default arises or to the long time provided for it in the agreement, it may be too late. My belief is that the road will in course of time become too valuable for us to act, -I think so highly of this transcontinental line owned by the Canadian Northern railway in connection with the new great policy for the settlement of the West-and I may deal with that question a little later on-that I have every confidence in the Canadian Northern as being a fine line of railway, because it has splendid connections and it would be the best possible asset that the people of Canada could acquire. Therefore I want to see some provision injected into this proposition which, while it would not in any way interfere with the agreement, would provide for the Parliament and the people of Canada acquiring this railroad.
At six o'clock, the House took recess. ,
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Hon. gentlemen who support these resolutions are fond of making comparisons between the present situation and that which existed when the Canadian Northern railway came to the late Government at different times for assistance. The late Government obtained first mortgages in every case, 1 think. But apart from that, it seems to me the comparisons are very unfair. The late Government appear to have followed the usual course in the assistance which they gave to this company. So far as I can find out they only gave such assistance as was usually given. As to whether or not such assistance should be given to railway companies, I do not propose to discuss that question	at this	time. I do not
think it necessary to discuss it.	The
situation at present, however, is entirely different. This company has received as much assistance as any company under similar circumstances has received heretofore. It seems to me that all things considered there is no great railway company in Canada that has received proportionately the amount of assistance for the amount of work done, or supposed to be done, that this company has received. It was supposed that the assistance they had already received was sufficient to enable them to complete these lines. But now they come to us asking for additional assistance,

asking for something altogether out of the ordinary. It seems to me that when they come for unusual assistance we are justified in asking that they shall give us extraordinary security or something out of the ordinary as equivalent for that security, and it seems to me that that is admitted by the Government, as they themselves ask not only for security but also for a large block of the common stock in consideration of the assistance given. So, we seem to be agreed on that point, that we are entitled to an extraordinary return, if you like to call it so, for the guarantees we are giving. I think we agree also in this, that the security the company is giving the Government is not sufficient. That may be denied on the part of the supporters of this resolution-that is it may be denied in words but it is admitted in deeds. They are prepared to give the guarantee, but the^-demand not only the security that has been given but also $40,000,000 of the common stock. But if the security is ample, there is certainly no justification for asking for the common stock. No man can justify the action of the Government in demanding that stock if the security is ample. So, I think that so far as that goes we are on the same ground and believe that the security is not sufficient. The question of what we should get in place of the security, or whether we should accept any return in the place of the security, is up for discussion. I admit, I do not like the sort of return we are getting. Of course, we ail have our prejudices, and I with the rest I confess, I do not like the business of note-shaving: to me a disgusting business. But that, it seems to me, is exactly the business the Government is engaged in. They say, in effect: Yes, we will endorse your note, but we must have a rake-off. Many of us, of course, have been offered that by people who wished us to shave their notes. But for my part, I do not like the business and would not go into it. And, as I would not go into it as an individual, so I will never consent that I and others, the people of Canada, should go into that business. It is a business we have no right to go into, there is no justification to go into it. And it is a rather undignified position to be in, I think, to say the best of it.
We are told that the stock of this company is to be fixed at $100,000,000, and the people of Canada are to receive $40,000,000, while Mackenzie and Mann receive the *other $60,000,000. That has been discussed
IMr. L. Thomson.]	.
at length and I do not wish to go over the whole matter, but there are one or two points that have not been dwelt upon and which I should like to mention. It seems to me that the position is very serious, I notice that the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) to whom we must look as the spokesman of the people of Canada on this occasion, is reported at page 3831 of ' Hansard ' as saying, in speaking of this $40,000,000 of stock which the Government is to receive:
There is every reason to believe that before any great length of time there will be a par value for that stock.
That is, in a very short time, that stock will be worth one hundred cents on the dollar. The Solicitor General proclaims this not only to the members of the House and to the people of Canada but to the investors of the world. Mackenzie and Mann are going to hold $60,000,000 of that stock. What are they going to do with it? The most natural thing is to sell it, especially when they have the recommendation of the Solicitor General speaking for the people of Canada as to its value. Have not the holders of this stock the right to go to investors and say:	This stock is worth one
hundred cents on the dollar; if you doubt it, here is what the Solicitor General has said about it. That should settle the question fairly well. The hon. gentleman is responsible to the people, and the people are responsible for the representations he makes, and investors are entitled to rely on such representations. The investor who buys these shares at one hundred cents on the dollar has the right to ask the people to see that he gets proper return for his money. What will the result be? The result will be, as we all know, that the people of the West must pay rates sufficiently high to recoup these investors and to give them reasonable interest on their money. I do not think that any company has ever had the advantage in going to the investor and the buyer of stock that this company has had; I do not know that any company that has ever existed in Canada has been so favourably situated. I am sure that no member of a Government has heretofore stood up in his place in the House and represented that the stock which is to be sold by any company in Canada is worth 100 cents on the dollar, as the Solicitor General has done. I am sure that the case is without parallel, and that the purchaser of stock in this case is in a better position to obtain reasonable returns on his invest-

ment than any other person who has ever before bought stock in Canada.
Although I followed his remarks very closely, I was not able to come to a reasonable conclusion as to what objections the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) was urging to the amendment, further than that in his opinion it would be hardly fair to bring the common stock down to $30,000,000. That appears to be the only objection the hon. gentleman has, so far as I could gather, to the amendment, because the amendment which he suggested was practically the same, except with regard to that particular phase of the matter. I think that he wanted to inject something into this resolution that the Government would accept. Of course, the Government are responsible for what they accept, but if the Government object to the amendment of the hon. member for St. John, they will oppose any other effective provision that it may be desired to inject into these resolutions; if they are not effective, of course, they are of no use. The hon. member for South York seems to be under the impression that Mackenzie and Mann would not be sufficiently paid for their labours if the amount of the stock were cut down to $30,000,000; the Government seem to be of the opinion that Mackenzie and Mann should receive $60,000,000 for their services. The Prime Minister refers to the lands which he appears to think Mackenzie and Mann are throwing in. I do not see that Mackenzie and Mann personally have anything to do with these lands, aside from the fact that they are the property of the Canadian Northern railway. The Canadian Northern Railway Company, not Mackenzie and Mann individually, have the right to those lands. It was because the railway was being built that these lands were granted, and if there is any benefit to be obtained the railway company should receive that benefit. Mackenzie and Mann as individuals, therefore, are not giving anything, so far as these lands are concerned.
I think I am expressing the feeling of the people when I say most respectfully that I do not believe for a moment that Mackenzie and Mann have never received anything for their services during the last eighteen years. I doubt very much whether members of the Government believe that. All these interlocking corporations were not produced for nothing. There was a purpose in view in the purchasing and acquiring of these companies, and that purpose was to rake in as much money as possible.
However, admitting for the moment, for the sake of argument, that Mackenzie and Mann have heretofore received nothing but common stock, it is urged that if the common stock be cut down to $30,000,000 Mackenzie and Mann will not be getting enough for their services; that instead of $30,000,000 worth of common stock they should have $60,000,000 worth for the.eighteen years of service which they have rendered in connection with the enterprise. If Mackenzie and Mann have received nothing for their services; if they have looked after the letting of contracts and have attended to the work connected with the undertaking and have received nothing for it, I admit that they are entitled to something. The question is, how much are they entitled to receive ? We are told that they have given eighteen years of their lives to this service. The present Prime Minister of Canada has given eighteen years of the best portion of his life to the public service. The Government propose to pay Mackenzie and Mann $30,000,000 each for their eighteen years of service; has the Prime Minister received that much for his services? Is not the Prime Minister entitled to just	as	much	as these gentlemen
are? He occupies a more important position than they do; he has been selected by at least half the people of Canada as the most satisfactory man amongst them to take one of the most important positions that Canada can offer to any man. He has occupied that position for the greater part of the eighteen years during which he has been in public life. What has he received for his services? I have not ascertained exactly what he has received, but I do not think that there is any secret about it. I think I am safe in saying that he has not received one per cent of the amount which it is proposed to give Mackenzie and Mann for their services in connection with the Canadian Northern enterprise. Let us take our hon. friend the Solicitor General, who has been termed by his admirers as a second Daniel come to judgment. I admit that he is a great worker and a capable man; we all admire him, although we do not think very much of the job he has made of this agreement. Let us compare his remuneration with the amount which it is proposed to give to these gentlemen. My hon. friend, I understand, gets a salary of $5,000 a year as Solicitor General of Canada and it is proposed to pay Mackenzie and Mann for eighteen years of service, $30,000,000 each.

The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong. When Mackenzie, Mann and Gompany own entirely the $10,000,000 stock and $10,000,000 bonds of Town Properties, Limited, that is what they put in. There is no fractional interest in anything they put in. They own the equity of redemption and that is put in. They own that entirely.
Then I am still right, because if they have bonds in certain properties they have only a fractional interest.

They own stock and
bonds.
That is a fractional interest.
What else can there be besides stock and bonds?

If they own the whole
property, without any other persons being entitled to stock or bonds or in any way to derive benefit from it, they are the sole owners. I shall not quarrel with my hon. friend on that because he will admit that there are very few of those properties in which they have an entire interest.
I say they are absolute owners of everything put in, and no one shares with them.
They are-absolute owners of the stock and shares, but the stock and shares do not represent the whofle property.
Yes, they do.

If they own the shares of these railway companies, which are called subsidiary companies, these shares only represent a little part of those railways. We only receive security on the portion owned by Mackenzie and Mann, not on the subsidiary companies. [DOT]
We do not take security on that, we take the security on the interest of Mackenzie and Mann in the $10,000,000 stock and $10,000,000 'bonds in Town Properties, Limited.

I do not think there is any need of taking up time on that because my hon. friend and I agree in reality, although we put it in different ways. Because they own unhampered shares in certain property, while they have a total interest in those shares they have not a total interest in the property; they only own a fractional interest in it. Therefore, I say, there is no good reason why other properties should not be included. We only want their interest, it may be good, 'bad or indifferent, they may own the whole of something that is very little use or a portion of something that is of great use. I think I am right in saying that the feeling of the country is that these companies are putting in the stock which is of very little use because of encumbrances and such things against the property and the things that are of use they are keeping carefully out, and are finding all kinds of excuses, which are accepted by my hon. friend for keeping tnem out.
I wish to discuss briefly the question of public ownership which is raised by this amendment. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for South York, as I always do to his progressive theories. I

am a little sorry that while he is so progressive in his ideas he is conservative in his vote, hut I am pleased to note that my hon. friend is improving because this session he has given some progressive votes as well as progressive ideas. We may hope the time will come when his votes will be generally progressive as well as his ideas, and we shall welcome that day. The right hon. the Prime Minister seems to be very much annoyed at any suggestion that it might be well for us to own and operate railways. There was a time when my hon. friend was not so frightened of the idea. The Prime Minister seems to be very much annoyed also that any gentleman on this side of the House should have changed his ideas in the least with regard to the matter. He thinks it a terrible thing that any hon. member on this side of the House when in office were not in favour of government ownership, but when out of office are inclined to be in favour of it. My right hon. friend is very fond of the tu quoque argument. It struck me that he was liable to have thrown at him the retort of our boyhood days, you're another. It seems quite appropriate that the Prime Minister should speak of the position of those who, when in office, are opposed to Government ownership, and when out of office are in favour of it, because I am sure there is no one who can speak of it more feelingly than the Prime Minister; he has been there and should know all about it. One of his supporters has said that on this question he has turned a sharp curve. The Prime Minister seems to think he should have a monopoly on sharp curves, and he considers it a serious offence when anyone on this side of the House tries to take a curve of any kind. The unfortunate part is that the Prime Minister takes his curves in the wrong direction; they are backward short curves. If any one should make sharp curves into line in favour of Government ownership they would be taking the proper direction. That is the only difference between them and the Prime Minister, he goes backwards and they go forward. It is better to go forward than to go backward.
The most serious objection I see toward the Government owning such institutions as railroads is that the public do not take their politics seriously enough. I think when you say that you have said all that there is to be said against Government ownership. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) will agree with me that that is about all you can say against
government ownership, that the people do not take their politics with sufficient seriousness, they do not look seriously enough on public affairs, they are not disposed to give to them the same careful and businesslike attention that they give to their own private affairs. One of the greatest arguments in favour of government ownership, and one that appeals most strongly to me, is that it will induce the public to take their politics more seriously, and if it has that effect it will be a great help, it will be one of the greatest blessings we ever had in Canada. If development along the line of government ownership, control and management of public utilities will have the effect of inducing the people generally to take their politics more seriously, to give the same careful attention to the public business that they do to their private business, it will be a great blessing. If my hon. friend's amendment is accepted and if it has that effect he will have very great reason to be proud of having done this much for the benefit of the public.

When my right hon. friend the Prime Minister rose to speak on the amendment he was rather caustic in his remarks with reference to the last clause of the notice of this amendment having been struck out. I thought at the time my right hon. friend must have a very short memory if he forgot how often the resolution was changed before it came to the House in its present form. We had to wait for some time, for several days, and there were several changes in the resolution before-

speechtext:
There are too many
hon. members carrying on conversations which are quite audible to me and which are inconsistent with the quietness and decorum which should prevail while a debate is in progress.

My right hon. friend also tried to construe the amendment into a proposition that the Government should operate the road. I am very strongly in favour of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John, because it is a businesslike amendment. It is treating the guarantee as a loan, and if Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann are capable of carrying this enterprise to final success, I do not think they should object in any way to the proposal contained in the amendment. I am quite sure that it is a business proposition: we propose that the Government shall have control of the whole stock,

excepting a sufficient amount to qualify the directors of the Canadian Northern, until such time as the agreement has been successfully carried out. The builders of the Canadian Northern cannot reasonably make any objection to putting their stock in the hands of the Government, as trustee, to be reassigned to them when they have carried out the agreement. That strikes me as being a reasonable business proposition that no borrower should object to, and we can only treat the Canadian Northern or Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann as borrowers. I am quite sure that no business man would construe the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John as asking the Government to take over and operate the road. It is true it gives the present and any future Government the option of taking over and operating the road within five years. It gives the present Government absolute control of the road and of the expenditure of the $45,000,000. I, for one, do not see why the Government should object to the amendment. They should be the first to want absolute control of the expenditure of that money, for the country is furnishing the means by which Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann can complete the Canadian Northern enterprise. As to the reduction of the stock to $30,000,000, I am not going to say that the stock is watered. My right hon. friend says that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have put a certain amount of land into the completion of certain roads in the West, but I do not agree with my right hon. friend that the lands from a moral business standpoint, belonged to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann privately. The lands were given to assist the completion of certain roads, and afterwards these roads received provincial guarantees sufficient in themselves to carry the roads to completion without the lands. Though Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann may legally have owned the whole of these lands, let me repeat that from a moral business standpoint the lands did not belong to them privately, but to the Canadian Northern railway. Therefore, so far as I am concerned I shall have to strike out these lands from what Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have personally put into the road. No doubt they have expended a great deal of energy and had a great deal of worry and vexation of spirit in connection with the construction of this road. But if, as the Prime Minister says, they are entitled to a claim against the road for the hard work and energy they have put into it I am quite 
sure that the $30,000,000 would be ample payment. My right hon. friend may not think so, but I am quite sure the people of Canada will think these two gentlemen are being fairly well paid if they get $30,000,000 for all their work and trials and tribulations in connection with the building of this road. The amendment of the hon. member for St. John proposes to reduce the capital stock to $30,000,000 and to give the present or any future Government the right to take over this road by paying Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, and paying them well, for all the trouble they have had. Personally, I would be' the last to say that they are not entitled to be well paid, but, as I said, they will be well paid if they get for their stock $30,000,000 or anything in that neighbourhood.

If I understand the hon.
gentleman, he does not consider the stock as absolutely worthless; as being all water.

I said that my right hon. friend had stated that the stock was not all water, and I also said that I disagreed with him as to the lands that were given for the building of certain roads in the West. I did not say the stock was all water. I said that these two men had put a certain amount of energy and hard work into the Toad and I am not saying that they are not entitled to a certain amount of stock for that, but I say they would be well paid if they got $30,000,000 for the work they have put in, and I am quite sure my hon. friend will agree with me in that. I think if he was one of these gentlemen he would be quite satisfied with his portion of that $30,000,000.

During the time the stock might be in the Receiver General's hands, as is provided for in the resolutions in case of default, are you in favour of Mackenzie and Mann or the Government operating the road?

I am in favour, and I
understand the amendment is in favour of Mackenzie and Mann finishing the work, but under the control of the Government. The instant the stock is assigned to the Government, we get control.
That is all struck out now.
No, it is not struck out; it is simply not definitely stated.
It was definitely stated and then struck out.
