Mr. Speaker, in pursuance of the notice given last night, I desire to move an amendment. I do not wish to repeat what I said last night in all particulars; hut I may repeat this much that, as the resolutions assume to control freight rates over this railroad system so far as to give a preference in rates to Canadian ocean ports, it would not be right that the resolutions should go through without an amendment being moved which, by assuming a measure of control over freight rates, would remove the inequality that now exists between freight rates in western and in eastern Canada. This railroad system will operate in the West and in the East. At the present time there is serious discrimination in railway freight rates in the West as compared with the East. I cannot consider that it would be right to allow this measure-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. There are too
many hon. members moving around in the Chamber and too much talking for the speaker to be heard. It seems to me that, having regard to the decorum of the House of Commons, hon. gentlemen when addressing the House are entitled to better attention.

I desire to say that on this occasion, when this railway company is being dealt with generously by Parliament, it is right and proper to impose freight rate restrictions and to exercise freight rate control over those parts of the line by which traffic reaches Atlantic ocean ports, it is just as right and far more necessary that, as a consideration for the assistance given, a like control should be exercised and the discrimination that now exists in regard to freight rates as applied to western Canada should toe removed, so far as this railroad system is concerned. It is desirable that we should have railroads; but the purpose of a railroad is, first to give accommodation, and next to give accommodation at rates that will make business profitable. Conditions at the present time are such, in view of the falling price of the main product of western Canada in the world's markets, that it becomes necessary to lighten by every possible means the burden upon production of that part of the
nation's wealth. The costs of transportation are a part of the cost of production, and a decrease in the costs of transportation is a decrease in the cost of production, and a corresponding widening of the basis of production. It is true that the through freight rates are not discriminatory. It is the local freight rates in which there is discrimination at the present time, and it is in regard to these local freight rates that we desire to have the discrimination removed.
It is particularly important, it seems to me, that .there should be a declaration toy Parliament upon this subject at this time. As has already been said during the course of this debate, this Government is taking a large financial interest in this Canadian Northern enterprise, a forty per cent interest in whatever profits may accrue. When the Government is taking a forty per cent interest in the profits and consequently in the earnings of the enterprise, the Government has a special interest in freight rates; and it is desirable before these resolutions are passed, before the agreement becomes effective, that the purposes of the Government should be defined and the mind of Parliament should be declared in what direction the Government will exercise the authority vested in it as a Government having control of transportation, and how far it will exercise the authority vested in it as a partner in the Canadian Northern Railway enterprise, to maintain its earning powers fox the purpose of securing dividends.
The conditions to-day are different from what they were three months ago. When this matter was under consideration in the House last year, we were told that the question of discrimination in railway freight rates was under the consideration of the Railway Commission. We were given to understand that it was a matter that was entirely under the control of the Railway Commission; that it was not a matter that should be dealt with or interfered with by Parliament. Since that time the Railway Commission, having taken the matter into consideration at great length, have delivered a decision which confirms that condition of discrimination in freight rates between eastern and western Canada, of which western Canada has complained during the past year. Clearly then, while the country reasonably might have looked to the Railway Commission for such an adjustment of rates as would have been fair

to western Canada, the condition to-day is, that we are past the point of looking to the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission has rendered its decision, which is against western Canada and in favour of discrimination in railway rates. The only authority in the Dominion of Canada that can put the question of freight rates between East and West on a position of equality is this Parliament. And it seems to me that now is the time and this is the occasion for Parliament to make a declaration that shall be effective so . far as this transportation system is concerned.
If equality of rates is established on the Canadian Northern railway system, it will, in effect and in practice, be established on the other and competitive systems doing business in the western country. It is because of this effect of the existence of the Canadian Northern Railway system as a competitive transportation enterprise, that it has claims, or may be considered to have claims, upon Parliament for favourable consideration. As a competitive transportation enterprise it has merit, and may claim assistance towards its maintenance. But, if it is not to give the benefits of a competitive transportation enterprise, then there is no good reason why it should be dealt with so liberally by the Parliament of Canada as is proposed in this resolution. Therefore, I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Buchanan:
That the said resolution be not now concurred in but that it be referred back lo Committee of the Whole for amendment, to provide that:
The Canadian Northern Railway Company shall within two months from the date of the passing of this Act, submit to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada a schedule of traffic rates upon the lines of the said company now or hereafter to be constructed west of Fort William, which shall be the same as now applies on the lines of the said company in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, except in so far and to such extent as the said Canadian Northern Railway Company may be able to establish higher cost of operation on such lines west of Fort William, and the said schedule shall be subject to the authority and control of the said Board of Railway Commissioners, to be revised and adjusted by them in accordance with the foregoing provision.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I do not know that under ordinary circumstances, so far as the amendment of my hon. friend is concerned, it would be necessary to make any reply, especially for western Canada, where the circumstances and conditions are well understood. It is undoubtedly true that the

transportation question is a very live question, that it is the all-important question with the people of western Canada. But let me say-and in saying it I do not wish to be misunderstood, I do not wish to be thought in any way discourteous to any hon. gentleman opposite-that in view of the many and varied statements made in the discussion on these resolutions, as well as of the many and varied amendments which we have had, it is desirable to realize and understand that the amendments of these hon. gentlemen are not regarded seriously either by this House or by the people of this Dominion. Especially is this true when they attempt to make it appear that they have some knowledge of the question of railway freight rates and some policy of railway legislation designed, as this legislation is designed, to contribute benefit and advantage to the common people. It is necessary to keep this fact in mind. It is necessary also to keep in mind the fact that though these hon. gentlemen had the opportunity for many long years of presenting railway legislation to this Parliament for the benefit of the common people, yet search their legislation from end to end, and I defy any man to find any legislation placed on the statute-books by these hon. gentlemen that carried advantages to the people of the Dominion in respect of freight rates. This is true of their record with respect to western Canada and it applies to the conditions suggested by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). That hon. gentleman undertakes to say that there is discrimination in western freight rates. Now, that statement being true, the responsibility and the blame rests more upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen opposite than upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. My hon. friend refers to the fact that it has been acknowledged by the Railway Commission that discrimination exists in the freight rates applied to western Canada. That may be true, and my hon. friend quoted here last night a statement emanating from the Board of Trade of the city of Winnipeg in which that body makes the special request of the Government that when the Railway Act is being considered by this Parliament consideration may be given to the suggestions which they make in regard to this subject of discrimination. When that time comes it will be the duty of this Parliament to lend consideration and to give ear to the views of that important body.
In respect of the motion which is now proposed by my hon. friend for Edmonton,

I would like to ask how it would be possible for this Parliament to undertake to legislate in respect to one company only ? That is really the proposal of my hon. friend. We have as every one knows, several railway companies in western Canada. When I came to Ottawa in the fall of 1911, one of the first things that engaged my attention was the question of the discrimination in railway freight rates in western Canada. At the request of the board of trade of the city of Winnipeg, I submitted this matter to the then chairman of the Railway Commission, which was the proper thing to do if I felt that an injustice existed as against western Canada. Let me read to the House the reply of Judge Mabee, then chairman of the Railway Commission, dated November 25, 1911:	[DOT]
My dear Mr. Rogers:
X beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 23rd, enclosing me a statement covering comparison of freight rates as between points in eastern and western Canada, and in reply I beg to say that I had a similar statement forwarded to me, together with a resolution of the Winnipeg Board of Trade, a copy of which I enclose. The Honourable the Minister of Railways had a copy of the resolution forwarded to him and he, also, sent his copy to me. I take the liberty, also, of enclosing you a copy of my letter to the secretary of the Winnipeg Board of Trade. I do not know that you bothered about looking through this comparative statement, but it is full of most capable and easy explanation. They take Montreal, Quebec, and Windsor, all lake ports, as the basis of comparison. Take, for instance, the rate from Montreal to Windsor, $2.10, as compared with the rate from Winnipeg to Side-wood, $4.25; the rate from Quebec to Windsor of $2.56, as compared with the rate from Port Arthur to McLean of $5.74; the rate from Quebec to Rossport, $4.29, as compared with the rate from Port Arthur to Walsh, $7.36; the rate from Windsor to Jack Pish, $3.53, as compared with the rate from Port Arthur to Crane Lake of $7.06. Between Montreal and Windsor, Quebec and Windsor, Quebec and Rossport, Windsor and Jack Fish, there is a water communication, and between these places steamers are continually plying carrying large packet, and other freight, in competition with the railway company, and if the. latter expect to get traffic, they must, to some extent at least, meet the rates of the water carriers..! However, I know that the western rates are high-possibly, in many instances, too high- and if the Winnipeg Board of Trade will formulate their plans, I will set on foot a diligent and active inquiry with reference to the whole rate situation in the three prairie provinces.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) J. P. Mabee.
That was the position which I found when I came here in November, 1911. I followed the matter up and finally succeeded in having an inquiry made into the question of freight rates. A decision in the matter was
given a few months ago; a decision which, to my mind, is very gratifying indeed to the people of western Canada. We had also the statement of Judge Mabee that although he had been in office for a number of years he had never had a request from hon. gentlemen opposite to deal with this question of railway freight rates. The question naturally arises: Why did not Mr. Justice Mabee receive a request from hon. gentlemen opposite to that end, if they were at all interested in the welfare of the people of western Canada in the matter of freight rates ? It is a matter of fact that hon. gentlemen opposite wake up to the truth of the condition of affairs in this country only when they are relegated to the place which they now occupy in the seats of the Opposition in this Parliament, and I believe that the people of Canada will see that they are kept there for many years to come.
We have had in western Canada a very serious condition in respect to the question of transportation. As far back as the year 1900 the Government of the province of Manitoba, realizing that it was impossible to secure anything in that regard at the hands of the federal Government of that day, undertook to protect the citizens of shat province by providing for a reduction in railway freight rates. If any one part of this discussion was more amusing to me than another, it was that part in which the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition rose in this House and undertook to take credit to himeelf and to his Government for having done much for the Canadian Northern, and for having assisted it materially in the province of Manitoba and in the other provinces of western Canada. Let me correct my right hon. friend. The Government of which he was the leader never guaranteed a bond for a dollar in respect of the Canadian Northern railway in the province of Manitoba. But, notwithstanding the fact that my right hon. friend and his Government did not do that, the Government of that province protected the people by providing legislation that has not cost the people of that province one single dollar. The net result is that, if you analyse the figures in respect of the amount that is to-day being paid in transportation, and add thereto the reductions which were exacted iby that 'legislation, you will find that that legislation is saving the people of the province of Manitoba, and has been saving them for the past ten yeaTS over $5,000,000 a year. That is legislation of which the Conservative

I just rise to say a
word or two in regard to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Edmonton to which the hon. Minister of Public Works has addressed himself in his own somewhat peculiar style. So far as the amendment itself is concerned, the minister has quite obviously evaded the crux of the question, and purposely I think. He has gone considerably into railway history in an endeavour to show that the Liberal party during its term of office did nothing for the people of this country in regard to transportation. No one knows better than the minister that that is not the case. He knows that his main difficulty in the province of Manitoba was with the monopoly which had been created by the Conservative Government of Canada when,they granted a charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That was the trouble.

We had no trouble at
all.

And that trouble was caused by the Conservative party and opposed by the Liberal party as strenuously as anything could be opposed. I do not want to take away from the Minister of Public Works one jot or tittle of credit to which he is entitled for what he has done towards relieving the situation. I believe he is entitled to some credit and to more credit than his confreres in the Government for the reduction in freight rates which took place in Manitoba, but it is idle nonsense for a man of his intelligence to say that the Liberal party have done nothing for the people of this country in the way of reduction of freight rates. The very tribunal to which the Minister of Public Works appealed was created by the Liberal party in 1903 under the Railway Act which is still in force. Why was it created? It was to overcome the difficulties which were cropping up here, there, and everywhere in Canada.

You never asked the
commission to deal with this matter.

That commission was
established in 1903 by the Liberal party to deal with the difficulties which were cropping up everywhere in the Dominion. The Railway Commision did deal with freight rates in every portion of Canada. I do not say that they dealt with the equalization

Will my hon. friend allow me? I stated that Mr. Lafleur, K.C., had pointed out to the Railway Commission, as +he hon. gentleman may see in the report, that the prairie and mountain section of the Grand Trunk Pacific would cost over $96,000 per mile, and he claimed that as the fixed charges would consequently be over $4,000 a mile, it would be impossible for the company to meet any reduction in freight rates.

I quite understand my hon. friend's explanation. I am trying to deal with the three prairie provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I think Mr. Lafleur pointed out in the same argument that the cost in these provinces would run between $40,000 and $45,OQO a mile, but that if the higher cost of construction in British Columbia were taken into account the average per mile would be about what the minister has stated. Why not give the shippers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta the benefit of the low rates and equalize it if you will with the low rate which prevails in the East? It matters not one whit to the man who has goods to ship whether they go over the Grand Trunk railway or the Canadian Pacific railway. What he wants is to get his goods to the head of the lakes and then he can route them as he likes.
The Railway Commission has dealt with the question recently, it is true. Is there any reason why we should not revise its findings at this moment? I am not a western man; I have no particular or special interest in western men more than any citizen. of Canada would have, but I see the force and the point of the amendment which my hon. friend from Edmonton has seen fit to move. Now you have your chance. The Government is in a position to-day, in making this advance or loan to the Canadian Northern, to say: we insist that a term of this agreement shall he that you shall equalize your western traffic rates with your eastern traffic rates, unless you can demonstrate to the Board of Railway Commissioners that the cost of operation is so great that it is impossible to be done. That is all the amendment asks; it is a reasonable request, and it is a request which will satisfy the people of the West. They know now the reduction- that the Railway Commissioners have made in freight rates, and unless the Canadian Northern can demonstrate to them that the cost of operation in the West is

greater than in the East there will be another cut in freight rates, and the rates between the East and the West will be to a greater extent equalized1.
That is an important point to the people in the West. It is idle for the Minister of Public Works to say that the Liberal party never tried during its term of office, to relieve the western shippers. Surely we offered them a solution of the whole question in 1911, a solution of the whole transportation problem, and nothing has been holding this country back so much as the refusal of the people of the country to accept that solution. There was another solution offered just last autumn when the United States Government proposed to give free wheat and wheat products, as soon as Canada would do the same. Now, let the Minister of Public Works, get his thinking-cap on for one minute. He knew that was a good thing; he knew that would solve the railway rate question, and he went to Winnipeg and proclaimed it as such. The Government and Legislature of Manitoba, by a standing vote, unanimously declared that it was a solution of their difficulty in the West, and I have no doubt that the Minister of Public Works was in close conference with the leaders of the local party in Manitoba when that resolution was
10 p.m. passed in the Manitoba House.
Then he came down here. What does he say now ?-that the Liberal party has done nothing. I have pointed out that we erected the machinery, we made it possible to bring these matters before the board, we made it possible for the humblest citizen of the West to be heard, we made it possible to secure the reduction that has taken place. Then we made it possible in 1911 to make further reductions, which opportunity was rejected by the people. Even during the present session we have tried, by means of free wheat and flour, to make it'still more possible for the people of the West to move the greatest of their products at cheaper railway rates than they can now do. For these reasons I intend to vote for the resolution. I am not a western man, I am not affected by it, nor will the people of my county be greatly affected by the result of it. It seems fair and reasonable, it need not hinder the bargain, it cannot injure the bargain, and it is so businesslike that I think it should commend itself to the Government.

Mr. Speaker, there , is an issue between the Conservative and the Liberal parties, as was pointed out by the two previous speakers. I do not pro-279
pose to enter into the merits of the dispute, but I have always, when the Conservative party were in opposition and since they came into office, put forward in my motions the proposition that there ought to be an equality of railway rates in this country, and inasmuch as I have taken that stand in the past I intend to urge it here to-night and to urge it with all the force at my command. No one yet has ever given me a reason why there should be a discrimination against the people of the West and in favour of the East. These roads are national roads. They have been largely built by national contributions and they were so built in order to serve all the people of the country equitably. Instead of that there has been discrimination against the people of the West in passenger rates, in grain rates, and in ordinary transportation rates. There is no complaint made now as regards the transportation of grain, but the inequality still continues in regard to general freight matters. My contention is that this inequality should not continue. We do not discriminate against the West in connection with any law in this country. There is equality of treatment under the criminal law and in regard to the postal rates. But for some reason this Parliament stands for higher freight rates, higher express rates, higher telephone rates, and higher telegraph rates for the people of the West. Why should that be? It is not fair to the people of the West; it is not just treatment, and as long as we continue it the people of the West will have a grievance.
What has been the history of this question? I give every credit to the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) for his efforts in regard to the reduction which he secured for the people of Manitoba, and which he secured at a time when concessions were given to this same railway company that is under discussion to-night. Assistance was given to the railway; the Government helped them to acquire the Manitoba lines and in return for that 'assistance then given, a reduction in rates was acquired by the people of Manitoba. The result has been that the Railway Commission has seen fit to extend to the provinces of Saskatchewan and iAlberta the same rights that Manitoba had and which were secured by the Act of the Manitoba Government. If that happened in that case why should we not adopt the same methods here to-night and secure equality of treatment as between the East and the West? As was pointed out by the previous speaker (Mr. Guthrie), if the construction



of the Grand Trunk Pacific and this railway has cost a great deal of money, that high cost has occurred in the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia and, if so why should these people and the farmers of the Wesit be treated as they are now being treated by the Railway Commission, and why should the commission which was created by this Parliament take the stand, without any instructions from this House, that there should be this discrimination.
There is such a thing as the strategy of statesmanship, and the strategy of statesmanship is in taking advantage of every occasion as it arises to remedy public grievances. This is a public grievance in the West. A railway is here seeking aid. That same road sought aid once in the province of Ontario, and a concession was got then that we ought to get here to-night. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) subsidized the Grows-nest Pass branch of the Canadian Pacific railway, and got some concessions in regard to freight rates, and there was a reduction. On other occasions there have been reductions obtained. I simply maintain the position I have always maintained, that when concessions are given to railways is the time to get concessions from them. They have been got in the past, and they ought to be got now. 'Especially is it our duty to bring some relief to the people of the Canadian West. They have high interest rates to pay out theie. Why should they be so stigmatized? Largely because Parliament has stigmatized the people of the West in regard to railway rates, the bankers demand higher interest rates in the West. That should not be. We should make it our duty to declare for equality of treatment for everybody. As a consideration of the assistance that we are giving here to-night, we can insist that this company shall give the same treatment to the people of the West that they are giving to the people of the East. It has been mentioned that we are dealing only with one case, and that it would not be fair to deal with one and not with the others. It follows, as has been stated, that if that applies to one, the othens will have to follow.
It is reported in the press that the Grand Trunk Pacific are to come here this session for some further assistance. Why not set the example and impose the same condition upon them also, if they come here for assistance. Probably both the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific will
get assistance this session in order to enable them to complete their road, and we should say, in giving that assistance, that they must give equality of treatment to the people of the West. There is nothing unfair in that. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company can stand the reduction, as we all know because its treasury is overflowing. If I was induced at any time to assist legislation through this House in order to secure the construction of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, it was based on the statements made in this House time after time that, not only would they provide additional railway service but they would provide competition for reduction of rates.

What about public
ownership?

I will deal with that when the Grand Trunk Pacific matter comes up. At the present time I am dealing with the freight rates, and the opportunity presented to the hon. member for West Peterborough and the rest of us to afford some relief to the people of the West. What do the people of the West want? They are in competition with the farmers of the United States. Freight rates in the UnitedStates are lower than in the Canadian West; and that being the case, there ought to be equality of treatment as between the United States and us. We have nothing to do with that matter; but we have the opportunity here and we should take advantage of what I call strategy of statesmanship, and every time these people come here for assistance, we should insist on a concession being given to the people of the West. If we did that we would get that concession, and that is the only way in which to get it. The Railway Oommisiom, for some reason or other, have seen fit, without the authority of Parliament, to set up the principle of discrimination. That principle is a fundamental one; and it should not be in the hands of the Railway Commission, a creature of this House, to establish that artificial discrimination. There must be equality for the people. The people of the West have paid their share; they are paying their share to-day, and they will have to pay their share in the future of the completion of this railway. They will have to assume their share of the default, should there be any default; they will not be let off with less than the people of the. East, but they will have to pay their full share, and assume the same responsibility. That

being the case, why not give them equality of treatment? The people of the West want relief of some kind. It is coming more and more to be a recognized fact that graingrowing in the West is only possible if the farmers of the West get every encouragement, and especially if they get equality of treatment. Now that we have three great transcontinental railways on our hands, we must find traffic for them; we must find a policy that will encourage settlement in the West. We want settlers in the West; we want people to come from the United States and from all parts of the world; but we want them to understand that, when we invite them to come to Canada, they are going to get the same treatment in regard to railway freight rates as the people get in other portions of Canada. Is that unfair or unjust to any one? In my opinion, it is not. I have never met any one in this Government or in this House who will say that it is unfair. The only men who say that this discrimination should exist are the railway men. This discrimination should not exist, and this Government should put it on record for the guidance of the Railway Commission that this discrimination should not be allowed to continue.
What is the discrimination?
There are higher rates imposed on certain classes of freight in the western provinces than are charged in the East.
Specify them.
A resolution from the Winnipeg Board of Trade was read here, within the last two or three days. I am not going into the details.
Just wild general talk.

The hon. gentleman says that the Winnipeg Board of Trade is guilty of wild talk. The hon. gentleman says that all these hon. members who represent the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and especially the province of Manitoba, were indulging in wild talk when they said that the rates in the West were higher than in the East. I believe the facts which have been presented, and have been admitted by the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission says: You must pay more in the western provinces, but they do not give a reason for their decision. It is the duty of Parliament to insist upon equality of treatment. I am prepared to 279J
say that, in order to get equality of treatment and to get the Railway Commission to do justice to the people of the West, even if it should involve a slight genera] increase in rates, Parliament would be justified in allowing the Railway Commission to impose that increase; but I believe there will be such an increase of business to the railways, and such a rush of settlement in the West, that an increase in eastern rates will be negligible. The cure of the grievances in this country to-day, and of the so-called slump in business, lies in the immediate settlement of the West, and in bringing a class of farmers there who will develop that country, especially farmers from the western states. You cannot expect to get settlers to come into the West from the United States when you tell them that, if they go there, they are going into a country in which Parliament allows the railways, which are national undertakings, to discriminate as regards freight rates. In order to get American settlers into the West, you have to give them equality of rates.
You ought not to interfere with the settlers in the West getting the market of the United States for their wheat. If you give them equality of rates and the opportunity of selling their wheat in the best market that is to be found, you will see a new boom and a new era of settlement come to our Canadian West that will restore and revive business and put the nanne of Canada in the forefront of the world.

The best market is in
Winnipeg to-day.

If the farmer thinks he will have a better market if he ha.s two markets, I am not going to interfere with him; but I am going to be guided by the Conservative legislation of the province of Manitoba, and I am going to leave it to the farmers of the West to say what they [DOT] want. This is a free country; free opinion is allowed in 'all portions of it, and no man is a judge of his own conditions and his own wants as much as he is himself. I cannot be charged with saying what I am saying here to-night for political effect. I have given some little attention to this question in the past. I have taken, the position against hon. gentlemen opposite time after time that it was their duty to secure this equality of treatment. They did not secure it, but the opportunity is here to-

night to get it. No injury will be done to the Canadian Northern oir to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Pacific railway can well afford to give equality of treatment. Therefore, we should take advantage of each opportunity as it arises when these railways come here for assistance. We should take advantage of the Grand Trunk Pacific coming here, as I believe it is going to do-and it is the special pet of hon. gentlemen opposite-and Parliament will be justified in compelling them to give what the people of the West aire entitled to, namely, equality of rates. Why should there he discrimination? Where is the member from the West, on either side of the House, who is in favour of discrimination? I have talked with the members of this House, on both sides, and I have read the papers of the West, and I know that everybody says that what they want is equal treatment. Why should not they get it? I have not been able to find out. The only people who set up a different claim are the representatives of the railways before the Railway Commission. But, as I have said, if they cannot themselves do business on a basis of equality, then this Parliament will be justified in authorizing the Railway Commission to make a readjustment that will secure equality. For it is not law, it is not justice, to place this stigma upon the Canadian West. Why that stigma was ever put upon the West, I cannot understand. But, if we are friends of the West, if we believe in a united Canada, we must demand equality before the law. Therefore, not out of regard tor any political party, but as a matter of justice, I ask this equality of treatment. To grant it means not only to do justice but to secure greater prosperity for the whole country. It means putting more heart into the man in the West who is raising wheat and selling it at a price which leaves him but little profit. If we can give him relief on freight rates, if we can put him on an equality in this matter with every other citizen in this country, it will mean much for the West of Canada. I give Manitoba credit for the action it took, and I give credit to the hon. gentleman who had a hand in it. But if this has been an advantage, not only to Manitoba, but has spread its influence also to the other prairie provinces, why should not we seek to secure for all three of these provinces equality with Ontario? The hon. gentleman's contention proves the case absolutely-outside of the statements he has made as to lack
of consistency on the part of certain politicians. But the issue is not the issue of consistency but the issue of justice and equality. In keeping with the stand I have taken in the past, and on the ground of justice and of the welfare of Canada, I say we should make this concession now in connection with the Canadian Northern railway. And if the Grand Trunk railway comes here with a similar request, we should make the concession in connection with that system also.

I do not rise to answer the remarks made by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), for I feel that those remarks are unanswerable; they represent the opinions of the western people, and I believe they represent also the opinions of Canadians generally who are interested in the welfare of western Canada, and therefore of the whole Dominion. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) boasted of the position taken by the Manitoba Government when it had occasion to deal with this railway. This particular railway came to the Manitoba Government for assistance, and that Government in giving assistance stipulated certain things, one of them being a reduction in freight rates. The Minister of Public Works uses this as an argument in opposing this resolution of the Opposition demanding exactly the same thing as a condition of granting the application of this Canadian Northern railway for assistance from the Dominion Government in this year 1914. His argument was an argument in favour of this amendment of the Liberal party in regard to freight rates. If it was good for the province of Manitoba to make a deal for lower freight rates in Manitoba, then it is good for the Dominion of Canada when giving assistance to the Canadian Northern railway to arrange for the equalization of freight rates in the West. That is all we are asking for, and I think the Minister of Public Works has shown that this is an opportune time to deal with that question.
Reference has been made to what this Government has done in the matter of freight rates before the Railway Commission. I would point out that the recent decision of the Railway Commission was a victory for the counsel engaged by the Liberal Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan. They were able to get equalization of freight rates in the prairie provinces, but the experts and counsel engaged by the Dominion Government were not able to secure the equalization of freight rates between the East and the West. The decision


of the Railway Commission was practically a repudiation of the arguments presented by the Dominion expert, Mr. Mueller. In fact, it was stated that Mr. Mueller contradicted himself throughout his evidence and that his evidence was of no real value as an argument for the equalization of freight rates.
The Dominion Government is now coming to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway. We are told that we are being supplied with certain securities; we are told that we are entering into a partnership by getting a certain amount of stock in this road. I do not think the people of this country look upon this as tangible or of any real value. But I believe the people of both the East and West would consider an arrangement with regard to freight rates as of some value in this arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway. If we are going to hand over assistance to the railways every year, why do not we get something from the railways which will be helpful to the people who are putting up the money to construct these roads ? I say this is an opportune time to deal with this road and to bring about a revision of freight rates that will assist the people in the West and bring about better trade relations between eastern and western Canada.

Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved third reading of Bill No. 169, to amend the Customs Tariff, 1907.

I beg to move:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of Ways and Means with instructions that they have power to amend it by striking off section 2 from the said Bill.
Section 2 of this Bill, which will be section 7 of the Customs Tariff Act, provides for the imposition in certain cases of a surtax and the maximum rate is fixed at twenty per centum ad valorem.
It is left, however, with the Governor in Cbuncil to fix the amount of
11 p.m. the surtax. Under the customs tariff as it at present stands there is a similar provision, but a flat rate is fixed and this statutory rate cannot be changed by the Governor in Council. The purpose of the amending clause is to give, as I have said, to the Governor in Council the power of fixing from time to time, as they may see fit, the rate of the surtax. I submit that this is not a proper matter to leave to the discretion of the Governor in Council. A surtax is in the nature of a penalty against nations which do not accord to Canada what is considered to be fair tariff treatment. It is in an open and standing notice in our customs tariff to all countries of the world that unfair or discriminatory tariff treatment against Canada is liable to bring upon them. the imposition of a surtax under the Canadian customs tariff. It being intended for that purpose, therefore, 1 submit that it is not a fit and proper matter to be left to the executive, but should rather be fixed by statute and 'be amendable by Parliament. That has been the position of affairs, and I do not think that there is any Teason for our departing from it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This legislation is of the character known as retaliatory; it is for the purpose not of aggression but of defence, and is to be exercised only in the case of discrimination of an unfair and unjust character against the products of Canada which become imports to a foreign country. The principle of the legislation -has been already recognized in the Customs

tariff of 1907, section 7 of which is as follows r
Articles which are the produce or manufacture of any foreign country which treats imports from Canada less favourably than those from other countries may be subject to a surtax over and above the duties specified in schedule A, such surtax in every case to be one-third of the duty specified in the general tariff in the said schedule A.
Any question arising as to any foreign country or goods coming under the operation of the provisions in regard to the surtax shall be decided by the Minister of Customs, whose decision shall be final.
The Governor in Council may make provision for carrying out the purposes of this section, and may, by Order in Council, from time to time suspend the surtax from application to the goods of any country.
In connection with this section. I desire to call the attention of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) to a statement which he made in this House last evening. He said in substance that under the provisions of the Customs tariff of 1907 this surtax could be imposed only by Parliament and that the only power that was given to the Governor in Council was to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the section. Further, he took exception to the legislation which is now under consideration on the ground that the Governor in Council could fix a surtax which, he said, should be fixed only by Parliament. My hon. friend the member for Carleton is a good lawyer, I must say in fairness to him that he usually looks up legislation to which he refers and I generally regard his opinion as valuable. But I would point out to my hon. friend that under the legislation of the late Government as found in the Customs tariff of 1907, the question as to whether a surtax is to be imposed against the products of a foreign country discriminating against Canada rests not with Parliament nor with the Governor in Council, 'but with the Minister of Customs. He will see that that is the case if he refers to subsection 2 of section 7 of the Customs tariff of 1907.

I have not my statement before me, but I am satisfied that my horn, friend will not find that I said anything like what he has just stated. I said that the minister or the Governor in Council has the power now to say whether or not there shall be a surtax on a certain produce, but the rate is fixed at one-third.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understood my hon. friend to say last night-if he says that l am in error, of course I shall accept
his statement-that the surtax could only be imposed by Parliament.
Mr. CARViELL: Oh, no. What I stated was that there was no discretion allowed as to the amount of the surtax, it being fixed by Parliament. Under the new Act, however, discretionary powers will be vested in the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: vious occasions, it may be 2, 5 or 10 per cent, but must not exceed 20 per cent. It is not 20 per cent of the rates in the general tariff schedule but 20 per cent ad valorem, so that if the tariff rates were, let us say, 30 per cent upon certain commodities, it would be open to the Governor in Council to increase such rate to 35 per cent or 40 per cent, but no more than 50 per cent. This provision of a more flexible surtax is not unknown in the legislation of other countries. Germany, Italy, and Japan,have similar legislation. In Germany, on dutiable goods proceeding from states that treat German ships or products less favourably than those of other nations there may be imposed by way of surtax twice the amount of the tariff rate on dutiable goods.
That is fixed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. And free goods may be taxed with a duty not exceeding 50 per cent ad valorem, so there is a mixed provision in German legislation.
Italy provides that goods proceeding from countries in which Italian vessels and products are subject to a differential regime, may be burdened with an increase of frontier duties up to 50 per centum of the duty inscribed in the general tariff. In the case of goods duty free under the tariff, the same may be burdened with an import duty up to 25 per cent of their official marked value.
Japan provides that with respect to articles the produce or manufacture of a country in which vessels or produce or manufactures of Japan are subjected to less favourable treatment than those of other countries the articles of such country may be designated by imperial ordinance, which shall be liable to customs duties not exceeding in amount the value of such articles in addition to the duties prescribed in the tariff.
As I stated last night, it is open to the Governor in Council to impose such rates as to him appear advisable under the circumstances. It might be extremely undesirable to impose a surtax of 33J per cent, which my hon. friend from Halifax has described as a flat rate. That might be a prohibitive tariff. It might be that the situation could be reasonably met by im. posing a surtax of a much less amount, say 5 per cent or 10 per cent ad valorem, or even less. The 20 per cent ad valorem clause puts it in the power of the Government to impose a higher surtax than 33$ per cent should they deem it advisable. My hon. friend from Halifax referred last evening to the Underwood tariff of the United States. This is not particularly germane to the discussion, because, as I have already pointed out, this legislation is general and not aimed at any nation. In
[Mr. W. T. White. 1
regard to the provisions to which my hon. friend referred, I find that the United States tariff item section 4, paragraph J, subsection 7 reads:
That a discount of five per centum on all duties imposed by this Act shall be allowed on such goods, wares, and merchandise as shall be imported in vessels admitted to registration under the laws of the United States.
Provided that nothing in this subsection shall be so construed as to abrogate or in any manner impair or affect the provisions of any treaty concluded between the United States and any foreign nation.
That is the section of the Underwood tariff. The Attorney General of the United States advises in respect to that legislation as follows:
The five per cent discount to American vessels only, which was the primary object of the subsection, cannot be given without impairing the stipulations of existing treaties between the United States and various other powers, and that consequently the subsection, by the' express terms of the proviso, is inoperative.
So that, in respect to that particular section to which my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) drew my attention last evening, it is the opinion of the Attorney General that it is inoperative. I should say, for the information of the House, that on March 6 of this year the Board of General Appraisers of the United States rendered a decision overriding this opinion of the Attorney General which I 'have just quoted. Extracts from the decision are as follows:
Hence we hold that even though this law is made operative to its fullest extent, and the reduction given of five per cent upon goods imported in American bottoms, it will not have the effect of abrogating or impairing any treaty. We, therefore, find that the law must be so administered as to allow 5 per cent discount from the duty on goods imported in American vessels. . . . We conclude that subsection 7 of paragraph (j) of section 4, Tariff Act of 1913, should be enforced according to its letter.
The concluding paragraph of their decision is to this effect:
We, therefore, as above stated, sustain the protests where the goods are imported in vessels subject to American registry, and overrule the protests where the goods are imported in vessels not subject to American registry.
An appeal has been directed by the Attorney General of the United States from the decision of the Board of Appraisers to which I have referred. That is the position of the matter to-day.
Mr. BOltDEN: Where does the appeal lie?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The letter under which the appeal is directed is as follows:
Treasury Department, March 14, 1914.
Sir,-The department is in receipt of your letter of the 7th inst., recommending that an appeal be taken from the decision of the Board of United States General Appraisers, dated March 6, 1914, G.A. 7540 (T.D. 34246) that under subsection 7, paragraph J, section 4, Tariff Act of October 3, 1913, a discount of 5 per cent should be allowed on the duties imposed by that Act on goods imported in American vessels.
In view of the importance of the issue, you are hereby requested to file, in the name of the Secretary of the Treasury, an application with the United States Court of Customs Appeals for a review of the said decision, in accordance with the provisions of subsection 29 of section 28 of the Tariff Act of August 5, 1909.
Respectfully,
(100201) Charles S. Hamlin,
Assistant Secretary. Assistant Attorney General, New York.
Is that 1909?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I presume that is the Act which provides the method under which appeals may he taken. This provision of the Underwood Tariff Act is, therefore, in the opinion of the Attorney General of the United States inoperative, but the Board of General Appraisers of the United States have ruled differently and an appeal has been directed against the decision of the Board of General Appraisers to the United States Court of Customs Appeal. I have made some inquiries about the matter and I understand that at present no discrimination is being exercised against Canadian imports to the United States carried in Canadian vessels. As I stated last night, this legislation is general in character; it- is not aimed at any particular nation. I have stated that this Government, and I am sure any government, would reluctantly exercise the power conferred upon it by the Customs Tariff Act of 1907 and the amending legislation that we propose, to make use of the surtax as against the products of a nation discriminating against its goods or against its shipping. But as my hon. friend evidently had in mind the section of the Underwood tariff to which I have referred, and as he mentioned it last night, I thought it might be of interest to the House that I should place before it the position of the legislation at the present time. We feel that Canada should have legislation providing for a surtax to be imposed in proper cases. We feel that the present provision in the Customs Act of 1907 does not go far enough. We feel that it is not sufficiently flexible. My right hon.
friend says that it is rigid and my hon. friend from Halifax says that it is a penalty. We provide that the Governor in Council may, up to but not exceeding twenty per cent ad valorem, impose an additional tariff rate by way of surtax upon the products and manufactures of any foreign country which treats unjustly the imports of Canada or discriminates unfairly against its shipping.

Is that a power which a government would desire to have? Would it not be better for it to be able to justify the imposition of the surtax by statute? Would it not be more peremptory in its application and operation because when once done under this Act it is done and that is the answer to the foreign country. Would not leaving that power in the hands of the Governor in Council lead to interminable negotiations with other powers before and after?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Whatever is done by the
Governor in Council is done under the authority of this legislation and this is the legislation of Parliament.
I have no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Parliament may say to the Governor in Council-in fact Parliament has said to the Minister of Customs: you may impose a surtax of thirty-three and a third per cent in addition to the present tariff rates, that surtax to be fixed, rigid, and inflexible, or Parliament may say to the Governor in Council, as we propose: you tnay impose a surtax but it must not exceed twenty per cent ad valorem. In both cases the solirce of the authority of the Governor in Council is Parliament.
Of course, there is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
In any event it will
be prohibitory. A surtax is practically always prohibitory, it is intended to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not say that, I
would not agree that it is prohibitory, or intended to be prohibitory. I would not lay that down as a general proposition.
I do not lay it down as a wise proposition, but I say that is generally the effect of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The existing provision for a thirty-three and one-third per cent increase on the general tariff rate iby way of surtax would not necessarily constitute a prohibitory rate. Take a fifteen per cent or twenty per cent general tariff and one-third of that would be only five or six per cent, which would make a duty of twenty or twenty-six per cent which is about our average rate on dutiable goods. So I would not say that the surtax under the Customs Tariff of 1907 which we are amending was prohibitory or was intended to be prohibitory, nor will I say that a surtax should be prohibitory. I think the Governor in Council, under the sanction of parliamentary authority fixing a maximum rate, might well be left in the exercise of this discretion which presumably would be exercised wisely and with great circumspection as against any nation with whom the Dominion of Canada was carrying on business. The presumption is that the Government would exercise that power wisely and having regard to the situation that had developed. I have expressed myself on more than one occasion strongly to the effect that this Government or any Government would be extremely reluctant to invoke the surtax but if a case arose in which the surtax would be invoked, personally I can see no gbod reason why it should be placed at a rigid inflexible rate, at one-third of the general tariff rate. I can see no good reason why it should not be made more flexible and why there should not be a discretion which the Governor in Council should wisely exercise upon a proper occasion and impose a surtax which would be less than thirty-three and one-third per cent upon the general tariff rate.

I wish to correct the
minister. I find in yesterday's ' Hansard ' the following:
Mr. Carvell: Why has the minister changed the provisions of the present section 7? Under the present Tariff Act, the surtax is absolutely fixed by Parliament at one-third of the general tariff. By the new Tariff Act, it is provided that the minister has the right to fix this sur-

tax, excepting subsection 2 which provides for the surtax imposed upon goods going into the United States in any but United States vessels. What is the reason for changing it from the positive Act of Parliament to*the discretion of the minister? Does it not leave the matter open for the minister to make one trade with one importer and another trade with another? Does it not leave the matter open to lobbying between the importers and the minister? I think the minister should give some reason for changing an Act of Parliament into an Order in Council.
Mr. White: I direct my hon. friend's attention to section 7 of the present customs tariff by which power is given to the Governor in Council. Subsection 1 of section 2 of the Bill now under consideration provides that the Governor in Council may impose a surtax over and above the regular duties to an amount not exceeding twenty per cent ad valorem. The difference between the two sections is this. Under the present tariff the amount of the surtax is fixed at 33J per cent which is a very heavy surtax. Take the case of goods dutiable at 35 per cent one-third of 35 per cent would be nearly 12 per cent. There is no power to change that. It may appear desirable to the Government to impose a surtax of 2 per cent or 5 per cent, but not one of 12 per cent. The tariff rate might he too high it might be prohibitive, with the surtax of 33J per cent imposed on the goods sought to be imported ; it might be so high that it would be prohibitive if such a rate of duty by way of surtax were imposed. The amount of the surtax will be left to the discretion of the Governor in Council.
Mr. Carvell: That is just the objection. If there be a surtax it is imposed for a purpose; it is a penalty. I object to the degree of the penalty being left in the discretion of the min ister. I think that if there is to be a penalty Parliament should impose it and not the minister.
Mr. White: The Governor in Council.
Mr. Carvell: Under the present law the only power the Governor in Council has is to withdraw it entirely.
So I think the minister was in error in construing the existing statute as meaning that the minister has the right to- say that the surtax shall be applied or shall not be. If it were applied it would have to be for 33i per cent of the general tariff. I do not feel that the comparison between the tariffs of Italy, Germany and Japan would [DOT]be fair as compared with the laws of Canada. We are in Canada a strictly democratic country, so far as the enforcement of our laws are concerned, while in [DOT]the three countries concerned there is quite a lot of autocracy left in their form of Government. Let me give one illustration in recent times which ill my j'udgment shows that if a surtax is in effect at all it should be a fixed surtax. My friend will remember that in the United States in 1909, under the Payne-Aldrich tariff, certain surtax provisions were made which were fixed; and when the President of the United States held that he had no option

but to apply "these, they were felt to be so serious that it meant absolute prohibition of a large portion of our goods going into the United States. The result was that the parties came together, and, by a mere fiction, by this Parliament making a slight change in its Tariff Act which amounted to nothing, the President held that he was justified in saying that the provision did not apply to Canada.
'Mr. W-HITE: Supposing the surtax provision in the United States tariff had been flexible and not inflexible, would the President have been confronted with that difficulty?

No, but the probability is that he would have imposed a small surtax and we would have had to pay it. It was a rigid penalty, and the President did not feel like imposing it; negotiations were entered into, and the surtax was entirely disregarded as far as Canada was concerned. Ilf you are going to have a surtax, make it a surtax, something which is positive and which every country will know to be the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it had been flexible, what would have hindered the President of the United States, if he deemed it proper, and the Government of Canada, if they deemed it proper, entering into some arrangement of the kind that was entered into.

I can only say that, under the laws existing at that time, under the views of the President of the United States, we are all perfectly well aware that Mr. Taft would have imposed a very small surtax, and the people of Canada would have had to pay it whatever it was. As it was, we avoided it entirely. It is, I think, another argument in favour of making the surtax positive, and not leaving it in the hands of the Governor in Council or the Government or the minister, or whoever the authority may be, to dicker backward and forward, and make one trade with one country and another with another.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The motion is scarcely in proper form, because, instead of being to refer back to the Committee of the Whole it is to refer back to Committee of Ways and Means. Some other slight informality, can, I presume, be made right by the clerk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I accept the statement of my hon. friend from Carleton as to what he meant by his remarks of last evening.
What misled me as to what he had in his mind was this remark of his:
Mr. Carvell: Under the present law the only power the Governor In Council has is to withdraw it entirely.
I understood my hon. friend to have it in his mind that Parliament must impose a surtax and that the only power the Governor in Council had was, as he has stated it here, to withdraw it entirely.
Or impose it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Evidently what he had in his mind was that Parliament fixed the amount at thirty-three and one-third per cent and that the Governor in Council had power to make regulations with regard to that. I understand him now to agree with me that the Minister of Customs can decide in what cases the surtax shall be applied.

The law which it is now sought to amend has been in existence for something like seven years. On the whole, I think it has worked satisfactorily. While Germany was the country of which we had to complain at that time, it has had the effect and the result *of bettering the conditions of which we had to complain against the German Government. Our relations, as a consequence of this, were placed upon a more satisfactory basis.
Before I go any further I may say that I have not heard my hon. friend state to this House what inconvenience he has found in the working of the Act which has made necessary this legislation? So far as I know, he has not cited a case in which the surtax of one-third of the duty has been found to be unsatisfactory, and wherein it would have been more conducive to the general welfare of the country if he had had the flexibility which he now seeks to have. Unless inconveniences are found in the working of the statute, it is always a better policy to leave it as it is.
There is one thing in the amendment of my hon. friend to which I have no objection at all to offer. He is now seeking to enlarge the scope of this statute and to extend it, not only to a case of the imposition of the duty to which it is now limited, but to meet the possibility of discrimination in the shipping of goods. So far, I am altogether in sympathy with my hon. friend, and I think it is a wise provision he is making to reach, not only the injustice from which we have to suffer in the case of an abnormal duty under the present law,

but to meet such a case as he has in mind of injustice done to us in the shipping of goods. If he had confined his amendment to that alone, and extended it simply to the shipping, for my part I would have no objection; but, on the contrary, I would rather commend his action.
To one point to which we on this side of the House take exception is the power which he takes from Parliament and gives to the Governor in Council of establishing the rate of duty. The surtax is a tax; and a tax ought to be fixed by Parliament and ought not to be arbitrary nor in the power of the Governor in Council to alleviate or to make more onerous. Every subject ought to know what are the taxes he has to pay. In a matter of this kind there is nothing to be gained but much to be feared if the power of fixing the taxation, at present vested in Parliament, is made over to the Governor in Council. I am afraid that under the present Administration there is too great a tendency to take away powers from Parliament and to give them to the Governor in Council. I believe in the view held on this side of the House, that this tendency should not be encouraged and that every instance of it ought to be met by our determined opposition. I admit that there are cases in which the Governor in Council may be properly vested with such powers. For instance, the present law gives to the Governor in Council the power to determine when the Act shall apply:
The question arising as to any foreign country or goods coming under the operation of this section shall he decided by the Minister of Customs, whose decision shall be final.
This is a power which is properly vested in the Governor in Council, which Parliament gave at the time and which ought to rest in the Governor in Council. The fact that a new Act shall be passed in Germany, or Japan or Italy or the United. States, discriminating against Canada, or imposing an abnormal duty or a surtax, such as we had to complain of in 1907, is a circumstance in which the Governor in Council very properly and wisely is given at once the power to determine whether or not the Act shall apply and whether or not there is any injustice done to Canada. So far so good; but when it comes to the fixing of what shall be the tax, what is there to be gained in giving the power of determining the rate of duty to the Governor in Council ? My hon. friend says there may be cases where the tax will be five or ten or twenty per cent. The statute says the law shall be the same for all, whether Italy,

or Germany or Japan or the United States. The law says, as to any country which deals unfairly with Canada, that Canada will retaliate in this way and will impose such a duty. I submit, with all due deference to what my hon. friend has said that this case should rest altogether upon what inconveniences may have arisen in the application of the statute; and that, as the statute has proved to be satisfactory up to the present time, there is no occasion to alter the law, especially if you desire to alter the law in such a way as to give the Governor in Council the power to determine the rate of duty that shall be imposed.

I do not desire to go over the arguments made by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and I will merely say that I cannot appreciate the force of my right hon. friend's contention. He argues that Parliament, not the Governor in Council, should impose a tax, and thus that every man in this country should know exactly the amount of tax to which he shall be subject. The very statute which as my right hon. friend claims was properly passed by Parliament, gave to the Minister of Customs the power to impose a surtax.
No, to determine the case in which the tax should be imposed, not to determine the tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What is the difference in principle between the two? There is absolutely none. It is true, as I understand the provisions of the Bill, that the surtax may be somewhat larger or perhaps may be somewhat smaller under this legislation than under that which it supersedes, but the principle is in no wise changed. In the one case as in the other the decision as to whether the additional tax, whether large or small, shall be imposed, rests entirely with the minister under the former legislation, and with the Governor in Council under this legislation. Therefore, there is absolutely no distinction.
When my right hon. friend makes the suggestion that there has been an increasing tendency on the part of this Government to assume to itself powers which ought to be exercised by Parliament, I would like to point out to him that in the Naval Aid Act of 1910, there are no less than twenty-two sections which confer powers upon the Governor in Council, and some of them	of a	very important character. I do not	think that any
Bill passed during the past three years

'affords so striking an illustration of the conferring of powers upon the Governor in Council as that which my right hon. friend himself then passed. If one cared to examine the statutes passed during the fifteen years in which my right hon. friend held power, he would find numerous statutes in which that same principle was carried out to its fullest extent. I am not criticising that. The tendency of modern legislation is to confer upon the executive powers which can he more conveniently exercised by the executive than by Parliament. It is not a tendency of this Parliament alone; it has been a marked tendency of legislation in the Imperial Parliament foT the last forty or fifty years. The complexity of modern affairs renders it necessary.
That remark may be true about many subjects, but not of taxation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not want to go over that argument, but I thought I had made it abundantly clear to every hon. member that the principle was not changed here at all. The scope within which the power can be exercised is changed, but the principle is not changed.
Nobody said it was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then what is the point of my hon. friend's remark? I think in Great Britain you can find illustrations of the exercise of power by His Majesty in Council under legislation fully as striking as the legislation which we are amending or as that which is proposed to-night. However, I need not labour that point. The only purpose for which I rose was to emphasize the fact that there is absolutely no change of principle in this legislation as compared with that passed under the Administration of my hon. friend. I do not see how it would be possible for Parliament to define these conditions. It was left to the minister in 1907, and under the legislation now proposed it is left to the Governor in Council.
Amendment (Mr. A. K. Maclean) negatived.
Bill read the third time and passed.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 11.42 p.m.
Friday, May 29, 1914.
